evidence.originalText:
We've found PMF and just tripled our revenue since Minicor (YC P26) joined Y Combinator. I did not think the in-batch peer pressure would work so well!

The batchmates are absolutely relentless - and being around them reframes what speed in startups can look like. Every group office hours we'd see companies who just started grow extremely fast which was so inspiring.

Our key unlock between pre and post PMF (which took 2 years of slamming our head on the table BTW...) was figuring out who exactly our customers were, what they were trying to achieve, and when it becomes their top priority (almost impossibly hard).

After finding that integrations to legacy desktop systems was a sales blocker for our customers, the final distinction that mattered was whether they (AI companies) were selling to enterprise.

That one filter let us ask much sharper qualifying questions, and it's how we tripled, because our customers have millions in pipeline they can finally unlock now that they can integrate.

An insane stat - something like ~300 billion human hours a year are spent just entering data into enterprise systems of record... ex: a nurse typing a note into an EHR, a clerk keying a claim, a warehouse worker updating inventory by hand. For them, it's currently physically impossible to use AI because these systems have no APIs.

It's been a lot of extremely tireless nights for the team to keep up, and as a founder it's been a challenge to switch mindsets between pre and post PMF. But we are so lucky to be in good company.

I'm extremely grateful to the team, our mentors, and everyone who bet on us early.

To a great Demo Day!!!

(pic from our launch video)

evidence.text:
I know many of you are waiting for 2FA. Same.
It’s taking longer than we hoped, so I want to explain why it’s not “just another roadmap item”.

Quick thing first, because I keep seeing confusion chatting with our users: HOT Wallet has two account types.

If you created your wallet early on, you most likely have an MPC account.
A non-MPC account is just a classic self-custody wallet.

Here’s the difference in simple words:
- With a non-MPC wallet, one secret controls everything. If someone gets it, game over.
- With MPC, there isn’t a single secret sitting somewhere. The key is split. Part lives on your device, part lives inside HOT Protocol’s MPC infrastructure. You still control the wallet, but it’s much harder to compromise with one lucky mistake.

One important detail: our MPC is not “centralized custody”. The nodes are independent, the protocol is built on top of NEAR One MPC, and it’s been audited by Trail of Bits.

And that’s exactly why 2FA matters.

2FA on top of MPC means: even if you get tricked by a scam dApp, or someone gains access to your device, there’s an extra verification step before anything irreversible happens. Think Authenticator or email confirmations, depending on what you choose. 

It’s not a “nice to have”. It’s the difference between “I clicked once and got drained” and “I got a chance to stop it”.
We’ve already seen real support cases where users had malware on their PC, but their HOT funds stayed safe because many drainers are built around the traditional single-key wallet model. They don’t expect MPC.

Now, the tradeoff. MPC accounts currently live inside HOT Wallet and the HOT Protocol ecosystem. That means you can’t always export them into random third-party apps until they support this account type too.

So no, 2FA isn’t just another step toward some date on a roadmap.
It’s the feature that makes HOT Wallet feel like a primary wallet, not a “use at your own risk” wallet.

evidence.text:
I left my job that I loved after 8 years to start something new. 

Previously, I was a VP in Equity Research at Bank of America covering Healthcare Facilities and Managed Care, and now I’m building the tools I always wished I had.

Today I’m excited to announce the public launch of Soria: an AI “Bloomberg Terminal” built for healthcare.

We’re backed by 𝗬 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗯𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿, the founder of GLG, and other industry insiders. We recently won 𝗕𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗹𝗲𝗙𝗶𝗻’𝘀 #𝟭 𝗡𝗲𝘄 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗩𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗼𝗿 award, and are already privileged to serve many of the largest banks, hedge funds, and asset managers.

Our pitch is simple: the research process is still too manual, time-intensive, error-prone, and disjointed. Soria pre-aggregates the most important public and private sources that healthcare analysts actually care about, turns them into an always-updated sector model, and alerts users the moment key data changes.

No more manually tracking everything in Excel or feeling out of the loop.

We are differentiated in three critical ways:

1. 𝗦𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗮 𝗶𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲. There is zero setup. From day one, analysts receive real-time updates on the most important datapoints, curated and reviewed by actual research analysts. Every day we add more sources, and the model gets better without users needing to lift a finger.

2. 𝗦𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴. We do not need to integrate into your bank or fund. We build the research and data layer ourselves, then deliver the output however you want it: our web terminal UI, MCP, API, warehouse sync, or even just email.

3. 𝗦𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲. Most “AI for Finance” companies help analysts work faster, but still leave the job of sector coverage to the analyst. At Soria, we do that work for you.

The result is that we consolidate $200k+ of healthcare services vendor spend, including Milliman, HMA, Mark Farrah, AHD, Daloopa, FactSet, and NAIC, into one platform, while also doing the work of another associate on your team without the training or churn.

If you would like to learn more, please reach out to me on LinkedIn, email me at 𝗮𝗱𝗮𝗺.𝗿𝗼𝗻@𝘀𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘁𝗶𝗰𝘀.𝗰𝗼𝗺, or book a call on our website www.soriaanalytics.com.

evidence.title: Launch HN: Rudus (YC P26) – AI for concrete contractors
evidence.text: Hi HN, we’re Rishi and Sahil. We’ve developed Rudus ( https: www.rudus.ai ), an AI-powered takeoff and estimation platform built for concrete subcontractors. Takeoff is the process of measuring and quantifying materials from concrete plan sheets. Rudus identifies every concrete structure (footings, walls, columns, slabs), pulls in related details, and eliminates hours of manual quantity calculation. Here’s a demo: https: www.youtube.com watch?v=PAMNDRWEdlI . The problem: Concrete subcontractors are the backbone of every building, but their estimating workflow hasn t changed in 20 years. Right now, a senior estimator opens a PDF, manually traces every footing and grade beam, then hand-builds an Excel spreadsheet with 300+ line items- volumes, formwork, rebar by bar size with lap splices and development lengths. Bids can take weeks and even months. Most firms have just a few estimators, meaning they physically cannot bid on most of the work available to them. The software incumbent in this trade hasn’t been updated since 2020. Beyond that, every AI takeoff tool on the market was built for GCs and treats concrete as one checkbox, rather than working around how concrete estimators actually price work. We’re building Rudus for this trade and only this trade. We started this when Sahil took a construction management class and realized how the estimation workflows hadn t changed in decades. We started cold calling, walking into offices with donuts, showing up at job sites, and everyone told us the same thing: slow estimation is the biggest bottleneck in growing their business, but every new product they ve tried has failed. We quickly realized that the reason those tools failed is a lack of trust and frequent errors causing later problems. Estimators stake million to billion dollar bids on these numbers, and they are clear that they won’t trade their workflow for a black box. We took a different approach: software that intelligently accelerates their current workflows rather than replacing it by forward deploying our product into their current estimation workflow. When an estimator uploads their structural PDFs to Rudus, we auto-classify every sheet (foundation plans, section details, footing schedules, frame elevations) and route each to the right processing pipeline. Computer vision detects concrete elements across the drawing set and follows cross-references across sheets to resolve dimensions and detailing, catching elements that plan-only tools always miss. Each element gets expanded into full assembly line items: concrete, formwork, and rebar with all the calculations an estimator would normally do by hand. A typical foundation package goes from a handful of assemblies to 80-120 priced line items. The estimator reviews, overrides where needed, and exports straight into their existing workflow. We have a couple key advantages in the AI estimation space. The first is our focus on concrete, a niche part of construction. No one else is building this for concrete subs because the sheets vary drastically from other subtrades. For this same reason, VLMs and other generic solutions don t work. Instead, proprietary computer vision models are required, relying on training from massive amounts of customer data. We run multiple different models trained directly on our customers takeoffs, and every interaction from our customers with our models becomes a training example, allowing accuracy per client to sharpen with use. Our second advantage is in our product methodology, as we’ve chosen to build a copilot, not a black box. Most AI takeoff platforms try to replace the estimator completely by autonomously producing quantities, but the quality of the outputs with current models is poor, so the takeoff gets redone by hand anyway. After 100+ hours sitting in rooms with structural concrete estimators and completing numerous takeoffs ourselves, we’ve built around their actual workflow. The estimator starts the takeoff, and Rudus extends the work across the sheet by finding similarities, following cross-references, and understanding callouts. The estimator stays in control of every accept, override, and edit. The result is faster takeoffs they can defend, not unreliable AI output they throw away. We’d love to hear what you guys think about our demo video ( https: www.youtube.com watch?v=PAMNDRWEdlI ) or your experiences building out computer vision models, or anything you think is relevant!

evidence.originalText:
YC Demo Day #2 is done.

$1k to $20k MRR in three months.

Runtime started as an idea I couldn't stop thinking about over the winter holidays.

Tokens were getting cheaper and models were getting better. My bet was that coding agents would go mainstream, well beyond engineering teams.

So I started building the infrastructure that was missing: a way for any company to let anyone in their org run coding agents without the usual setup and engineering handholding.

The roadmap was clear from day one. Let anyone at a company spin up an agent that already knows their team's best practices.

That meant more than a context layer. We built the execution, orchestration, and observability layers too, so people can run agents from wherever they already work. Whether that's Slack, Linear, API, or CLI.

Today we're working with companies from Series A to unicorns, running thousands of agent sessions a week.

What began as a solo open source project is now the work of Carlos Volante, Manuel Angel Hakim, Peter Barron, and the customers and investors who've helped turn Runtime into something hundreds of people use every week.

And this is just getting started.

evidence.title: What an incredible few weeks at Y Combinator.
evidence.text:
What an incredible few weeks at Y Combinator. Quick observations of SF, the batch and Modern:

- The density of young builders here operating with both pace and maturity is wild. For any young entrepreneurs, book that flight and put yourself in this environment.

- Great companies are built on embodied optimism and being surrounded by it daily is energising.

- The perceived pace of AI change settles once you see a clearer path of what will float and what will sink. There's a lot of noise. The noise will eventually stop.

- Friday runs are a win with the YC crew. Charlie Warren and Mathilde Collin leading from the front.

- Birthday's in SF are special when friends fly in to celebrate.

- The pull of Modern (YC P26) has been incredible. Aleks Tomovski and I running hard across time zones and teams pushing to go-live ASAP. 

- Waking up with more energy than I did when I was 18; enjoying all the vicissitudes.

evidence.title: Taro Fukuyama new investment: Apollo Atomics
evidence.text:
🎉 New Investment: Apollo Atomics (YC P26) 🎉
I'm excited to share that I'm investing in Apollo Atomics alongside Y Combinator and Pioneer Fund.
Apollo Atomics builds compact nuclear reactors for customers who can't wait for the grid. Conventional nuclear takes over a decade and roughly $20B per plant, while most SMR startups bet on exotic fuels and supply chains that don't exist yet. Apollo keeps the pressurized water reactor technology that already powers 80% of the world's nuclear plants and redesigns just one component, the steam generator, making the plant roughly 80% smaller without compromising power. The result is a factory-built reactor that fits on a truck and deploys in under 24 months, serving data centers, industrials, and utilities. They've already built and tested a working demonstrator.
Co-founder and CEO Assil Halimi holds a PhD in Nuclear Engineering from MIT, with 18 peer-reviewed publications and two patents on reactor design. He previously worked in reactor operations at Engie and an advanced reactor designer with EDF, the world's largest nuclear operator. Co-founder and COO Drew Walker previously co-founded Blue Innovations Group, an electric boat startup, and served in the White House. Deep nuclear engineering credibility paired with commercial and operations execution. Exactly the team this industry needs.
Let's goo!

evidence.text:
🎉 New Investment: Superset 🎉
I'm excited to share that I'm investing in Superset alongside Y Combinator and Pioneer Fund.
Superset is the open-source, terminal-first IDE built for the AI agents era. As developers shift from writing code line by line to orchestrating coding agents like Claude Code and Codex, the old text-editor model breaks down. Superset lets engineers run multiple agents in parallel, automate workflows, aggregate context from tickets and logs, and review changes fast.
The traction is remarkable. In just five months since launch, Superset has crossed 11K GitHub stars with 75+ contributors and become a daily driver for engineers at OpenAI, Google, and Vercel, along with major open-source projects like Homebrew and browser-use. It hit number one on Product Hunt and reached the top four on Hacker News twice, backed by a fast-growing community.
The team behind it is Avi Peltz, Kiet Ho, and Satya Patel. They are building exactly where software development is heading and have already shipped a product that the best engineers love and use every day. They move fast, listen closely to their community, and have earned deep conviction from top builders across the ecosystem. I'm thrilled to back them.

evidence.title: Reliability in high-stakes work
evidence.text: I've noticed a change this YC batch. A year ago, everyone was building agents. That made sense. Agents made every workflow look automatable. But in high stakes work, mostly right is not good enough. The companies pulling ahead are figuring out how to do the work reliably enough that customers can actually trust the output. This is fundamentally how we think about product at Arden (YC P26). Internal audit is one of those markets where the output must be reliable. The workflows are messy, the details matter, and teams need to trust the system before they let it touch real evidence. Curious if other people are feeling this too.

evidence.text:
5.6M of you saw the launch film.
It was shot on 16mm film. Not AI generated.

We fundamentally disagree with the direction technology is pushing creativity towards.

We're building a company about human emotion, presence, and connection. We spent days in the desert with actual humans creating something together.

That moment when a group of people all lock in behind a shared vision is one of the most fulfilling human experiences.

The essence of happiness is creating together.

AI is incredible. We use it internally all the time. But there's a difference between using AI as a tool and using it to replace human craftsmanship.

Right now, a lot of creative work is starting to feel optimized and generic. Perfectly generated. Perfectly forgettable.

We wanted to make something that felt alive and nostalgic.

Technology should not remove humans from the equation. Instead it should make us feel more human.

That belief is at the center of Anoria. Not just in our product, but in how we build, design, communicate, and create together.

evidence.text:
Two months ago I was going to sleep at 4 am and waking up at 7:30 after working on Datost (YC P26) after my 9 to 9 job. I genuinely could not stop. The problem was too obvious and nobody was solving it right.

The Y Combinator call was music to my ears because it meant more people believed the vision. Jason Wang and I both quit our jobs the next day. No hesitation.

We're building Datost because every company is sitting on answers they can't access. Not because the data isn't there but because LLMs don't understand your business. Datost fixes that. It learns your context, your metrics, your definitions so you can just ask questions and get real answers. It will even track your metrics for you and investigate when they fall.

If your team is still waiting on analysts or drowning in dashboards, come talk to me. DMs are open.

evidence.originalText:
I’ve known Oskar Kwaśniewski for 5 years.

We met when I was 15, working at a small Polish company. We had no clue what mobile or React Native really was, but we somehow had two apps to maintain.

So we learned it together.

Then we both joined Callstack, which was a game changer for us. We got to work with many US-based clients and learned how great developer tools are built.

Over the last 5 years, we worked together across 3 different companies.

At some point, we knew we wanted to build something ourselves.

We tried a few things. B2C apps, consumer products, random ideas.
Most of them failed.

But we knew one thing: we understood dev tools, and we cared a lot about building the best developer experience.

So we applied to YC.

We got in, Pete Koomen gave us a chance, and today TesterArmy (YC P26) serves 40+ companies, from seed-stage startups to unicorns, helping them make sure their web and mobile products actually work.

The best part is that this still feels early.

There’s so much more we want to build! :)

evidence.title: My cofounders Alex and Martin already shared the polished, professional updates about Korso (YC P26) getting into Y Combinator, so I’m here to share the reality of our decision-making skills.
evidence.text:
My cofounders Alex and Martin already shared the polished, professional updates about Korso (YC P26) getting into Y Combinator, so I’m here to share the reality of our decision-making skills. 

For our drive up to SF from Orange County (that's normally a 7 hour drive), we decided to take the scenic route through Big Sur, thinking it would be a quick one hour detour. 14 hours later, we finally arrived. 

That drive is exactly what building a startup feels like. There's always bumps in the road. The path forward is never as straight as you expected and sometimes you have to stop and re-navigate, but at least the view along the way is incredible. 

We took a much more intentional detour right after getting accepted into the P26 batch. Martin, Alex, and I immediately packed our bags and spent the last two months living out of suitcases. We wanted to make sure the AI we are building for manufacturers actually solves their on-the-floor problems, not just our Silicon Valley assumptions. 

We're finally back, settled in SF, and building at full speed. Follow along to see how we bring modern AI to the manufacturing world. 

Just don't ask us for road trip directions.

It's cognitively impossible to do reliably. If a fleet can complete just 10 more jobs a day, that's worth millions per year. The opportunity cost of bad scheduling is enormous and almost nobody in this industry has solved it. Dayjob sits on top of existing ERP software. evidence.originalText:
Time to introduce my co-founder, Carlos Volante .

The intro is overdue. Carlos is Runtime’s CTO.

We met through a mutual founder friend in the fintech space a few years ago. Since then we’ve spent many weekends talking about agents, building side projects, and teaming up at hackathons.

At the last hackathon we did, Carlos and I shipped 6 full-stack apps in under 8 hours. We saw the potential of coding agents, but also the lack of infrastructure to make their output useful to others. We haven’t stopped obsessing over fixing that since.

Before Runtime, Carlos built custom agents and fine-tuned LLMs at Modern Treasury. Before that, he built platform and DevOps systems that served Fortune 500-scale infrastructure at Hulu and Finix .

Carlos is the best engineer I’ve worked with. He ships fast and can get low-level into infra. He’ll also sit in a customer meeting, speak the customer’s language, spot an upsell, and close it. Right now he’s running sales pitches while I start fundraising.

Lucky to be building alongside Carlos.

evidence.title: SF is the best place to build a huge company, that's why I moved here to build Zolvo
evidence.text:
SF is the best place to build a huge company, that's why I moved here to build Zolvo

I've been going back and forth to the Bay for the last three years. 

Why?

I was making things happen.

Reaching out to founders and investors I admired, grabbing coffees, coworking, finding any possible excuse to learn more.

3 years ago, there were not many latinos in tech around.

Things are changing for the better now.

Latam founders are building global companies.

No permission asked. No more thinking small. 

It's amazing to see events like Latam at Silicon Valley bring together the founders that are changing history back in Latam with the vibe that only SF has.

See you there?

Happy to join you Laura, Maria Echeverri & Nicolas!

evidence.authorName: Above her, the city keeps rising. Below her hands, something smaller is growing too. Neither one asks the other's permission. They just happen at the same time, on the same rooftop. No skyline was built by a machine working alone. Every beam went up because a person made a judgment call only a person could make. What's growing in her hands took the same kind of judgment, just quieter, learned the same ordinary way it always has: soil, water, attention, repeated until it becomes instinct. Machines need exactly what she already has. Not her labor. Her judgment, recorded, so a machine can finally learn from it. Human to Machine Symbiosis.

evidence.originalText:
Everyone asks why I did Y Combinator twice.

My response: I can't think of a reason *not* to.

To be in a YC batch is the experience of a lifetime. And I get to do it twice?

In 2015, Circle Medical went through YC. We grew it past $100M in annualized revenue.

By the time I started Clara, people assumed I'd skip the batch this time.

Repeat founder. Already had the network, the playbook, the scars. Made no sense to them. Made all the sense to me.

Here is how I think about what YC actually is. It's three things:

Advice. Most of it is freely available. Read PG's essays. Watch the YC videos. It's all there. (Though somehow it feels like most founders don't follow it.) What you cannot get anywhere else is office hours with Garry Tan or Tom Blomfield, tailored to your exact situation, on your exact week.

Community. This is the gold. Once you're in, you're in for life. And this time I get to open that door for Caitlin S. and Zeeshan Ahmed. That alone is worth it.

Demo Day. An impossible concentration of activity if you're fundraising. We were fortunate to raise before our batch this time, and it still did not change the value.

There are a surprisingly large number of repeat founders in any batch, including some with one or more exits. Not one of them has told me YC failed to add 7.53% to their valuation. Not one. Purely on that math, why would you not?

So what's it like now, compared to 2015? Strinkingly similar, yet different at the same time.

What's the same: Office hours feel identical. Small group, sharp questions, no fluff. The talks feel the same. The network and the community feel the same. YC has managed to scale the magic of the core program by keeping true to its value and roots, and adding group partners (who not coincidentally are all YC alum).

What's different: Scale. We had around 100 companies in our batch in 2015, and everyone thought that was enormous. This time it's about 200. You feel it most in the batch-wide talks and events. Demo Day in 2015 was at the Computer History Museum. Now it happens across three YC buildings with the roads blocked off to traffic. It feels like a block party.

One of the things that may not (yet) be evident from the outside is the institution YC has become, generating immense affinity and loyalty on the part of founders. YC is now compounding and I think many will be surprised a decade from now to see how this institution will play a role in shaping the economy, politics and beyond. But that's a story for another day.

See you at demo day!

Squeezed in a selfie with Garry Tan, Paul Graham, and Jessica Livingston at YC! 📸😁

Growing up, I used to read Paul Graham’s essays like they were scripture.

I watched every YC talk on YouTube. Read everything I could find about how he and Jessica built it from nothing. Two people who just believed the best founders were out there, overlooked, underestimated, and decided to bet on them anyway.

They shaped how I think. How I build. How I see the world.

This week, they came to YC to give a talk.

And I was sitting in the room.

After years of reading the words on a screen, I got to hear it in person. The early days. The doubt. The sheer amount of hardwork behind everything that looks inevitable in hindsight.

It reminded me that nothing starts polished. Everything great starts somewhere small and uncertain and a little scary.

We are 8 days from Demo Day. @saudara.ai let's goo! 🚀

Somewhere became here.

evidence.title: Taro Fukuyama new investment: Adialante
evidence.text:
🎉 New Investment: Adialante 🎉
I'm excited to share that I'm investing in Adialante alongside Y Combinator and Pioneer Fund.
AAdialante builds compact, mobile whole-body MRI to make cancer screening accessible to everyone. MRI is the best tool for catching cancer early, yet machines cost millions and need specialists, so patients get scanned only when it's too late. Adialante rebuilt MRI from the physics up — half the hardware, 80% lighter, whisper-quiet, full diagnostic quality. They don't sell machines; they operate them as imaging clinics on wheels, starting with prostate cancer. They already have $12.75M in LOIs and a first system scanning by demo day.
Founders Efraín Torres, PhD and Parker Jenkins are why I'm backing this. Both biomedical engineers, they met as students and spent six years inventing new MRI methods, winning millions in grants and securing patents. They pair deep technical skill with a sharp commercial wedge and the resolve to disrupt the industry.

evidence.originalText:
Recently, I made one of the biggest and most exciting decisions of my career - I joined Revanth Bodepudi as co-founder and CTO of Prototyping.io

After spending years building software, including AI systems at Microsoft and various startup and research roles, one thing always stood out to me: software teams can move incredibly fast, but hardware teams are still stuck dealing with slow, fragmented processes just to get a part made.

That gap felt solvable.

Going from an idea to a real, manufactured part still takes too many steps, too many back-and-forths, and too long. Engineers deserve better tooling.

Our goal is simple: to help hardware teams move from idea to real products faster and more reliably.

We're building fast and excited to share more soon. If you're working on hardware products or in the mechanical engineering community, we'd love to hear about your experience!

evidence.text:
A new release landed for smol machines with v1.5.0.

1. CUDA support, through api-remoting. This is pretty unique work because I don't think any existing options are doing this today. This basically enabled the local <-> remote GPU support meaning you can change and end point and ship your GPU workloads pointing to a remote GPU. There's also significant opportunities to further optimize with this approach. Idea for this came from a 2022 talk, consider this very experimental tech.

But imagine you being able to run any inference/training workloads local/remote with basically NO setup once the .smolmachine file is pre-baked.

2. Windows 10/11 support, is now out of beta! (There are some functionalities missing, ex CUDA support)

https://github.com/smol-machines/smolvm/releases/tag/v1.5.0

evidence.originalText:
In the 48 hours after Y Combinator posted our launch video, we got 15K page views.

Kinro (YC P26) had ~500 conversations on our insurance chat, hundreds of messages across SMS, WhatsApp, and email, and 30 inbound calls to our AI voice agent.

We closed two policies from these leads.

Visitors asked about coverage, pricing, eligibility, tradeoffs, and what protection made sense for them.

We also saw the other side of launching AI on the internet: people trying to jailbreak the models, get them to generate code, or push them into giving wrong coverage explanations.

That’s the real challenge.

The future of insurance buying will be conversational. People will talk to AI the same way they would talk to an expert broker.

But to make that safe, compliant, and trustworthy, you need more than a good model. You need insurance domain expertise, rigorous engineering, and a deep focus on customer protection.

That’s what we’re building at Kinro (YC P26): AI-native insurance distribution, built by a team with backgrounds in autonomous vehicle safety and AI.

Insurance is going conversational. We’re making sure it goes there safely.

evidence.originalText:
My face when someone asks me if I had fun in SF.

In all seriousness, Demo Day and the P26 batch is behind us now and I feel lucky to have been a part of it.

As we head back to New York and continue building Cohesion, there are a few things I am thinking about:

1. Have an outlandish vision: We were lucky to meet and hear from some incredible people during the batch including Chesky, Altman, and Graham, and my main takeaway: no one gets very far by dreaming about being number two. As Garry kept saying, "boil the ocean."

2. Nobody cares: Launch early and launch fast. Build like no one is watching because in the early days, no one is. Use your speed and freedom as your strength.

3. Make something people want: Growth, revenue, and any other metric is a proxy for real value, which is making something people want. Cohesion saw a step change in our metrics once we narrowed our focus and honed in on making something people want.

With YC done, what is the next step for Cohesion (YC P26)? Building a generational company alongside our customers. Onwards.

evidence.title: Taro Fukuyama new investment: Complir
evidence.text:
🎉 New Investment: Complir 🎉
I'm excited to share that I'm investing in Complir alongside Y Combinator.
Complir is AI-native compliance infrastructure for global retailers — Vanta for physical products. Selling across markets is brutal: rules differ by country, documentation is fragmented, and regulations shift constantly, so every launch becomes a fire drill. Complir maps products to the right regulatory requirements, turns messy product data into audit-ready records, and auto-generates labels, warnings, risk assessments, and technical docs. evidence.title:
⚰️ The open web is dying. Not slowly

NYT in court. Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default. Reddit paywalled to everyone except Googl...
evidence.text:
⚰️ The open web is dying. Not slowly

NYT in court. Cloudflare blocking AI crawlers by default. Reddit paywalled to everyone except Google and OpenAI.

Cloudflare's CEO said bot traffic will exceed human traffic by 2027. If your AI strategy depends on scraping the public internet, you have 18 months before your pipeline breaks.

Three strategies survive:
1/ Licensing deals. $200M checks to News Corp and Reddit. Only frontier labs can play.

2/ Synthetic data. Works for math and code. Collapses on everything else.

3/ Consented crowdsourced collection. Real people, real conditions, paid directly, auditable

The first two have hard ceilings. The third compounds.

Every contributor expands the languages, locations, and modalities you can serve. It works the way search worked in 2001 and mobile in 2009.

This is the bet at @hubxyz. 150+ countries already collecting what frontier labs can no longer scrape. Audio, image, video, text. With consent. With provenance.

The scrapers will keep fighting the lawsuits. The licensing deals will keep getting more expensive.

And quietly, the companies that invested in real collection infrastructure will become the only pipe that still works.

evidence.authorName: She puts the strap on the way she always does, one hand steadying it while the other reaches for something on the ledge. It takes a few seconds, no different from checking a watch. The dog is already close, ears up, because he knows what's coming. She crouches low, under the laundry line still hung with yesterday's wash, a small piece of food held between two fingers. She doesn't just hand it over. She waits half a second, judging when his mouth is actually ready, then lets go. He takes it too eagerly, the way he always does, and she laughs under her breath, not really meant for anyone. Nothing here was staged. It's a courtyard, a dog, a Tuesday like most others: buckets doing double duty as planters, tiled floor worn smooth in patches, a gate left open to the street. For a few minutes, a small camera on her head is quietly recording exactly how she does it, the crouch, the half-second wait, the precise release nobody taught her, she just knows. Somewhere far from this courtyard, that ordinary rhythm is becoming something else. Human to Machine Symbiosis.

evidence.title: From the cover of Nature to the agents of Netter (YC P26).
evidence.text:
From the cover of Nature to the agents of Netter (YC P26).

During my internship at AMOLF (Amsterdam), I wrote an algorithm that made the cover of Nature.

The lab was drowning in data: a single fungus generated ~700 GB of microscope images in two months, and a full experiment meant tens of terabytes a month. They could only study a handful of these organisms, by hand.

I built an algorithm to fix that: turn thousands of images into one compact map of the network, with the exact moment each branch grew baked in. Around 1000x smaller, and for the first time the team could analyze the entire dataset.

The network (every branch colored by its age) got featured on the cover of Nature.

That experience inspired me to build Netter (YC P26).

No matter how smart the LLM, what limits us is getting messy information into a shape intelligence can actually use.

Most companies have the exact same problem, at scale. Years of valuable data, scattered across tools that don’t talk to each other, and teams analyzing a sliver of it by hand.

Our mission is to democratize data science excellence: normalize and organize data so AI agents can reason across it and deploy the right intelligence for each situation.

We are now applying the same approach to entire companies (instead of fungi), with results already in production.

And we’re just getting started.

evidence.title: Robots won't fail because they can't see - they will fail because they can't feel
evidence.text:
Robots won't fail because they can't see - they will fail because they can't feel.

The sense of touch allows us to differentiate between picking up a plastic wrapper and a phone. It's the reason we're able to work with objects of all shapes, sizes, and structures. Without this information, robots are operating blind in the physical world.

At Intelligence Factory, Jalaj Shukla and Julien Stocker are building data collection hardware that captures force and tactile feedback from human demonstrations. With this, our models generalize across a wide range of objects.

If you're an engineer passionate about robotic intelligence and want to help solve this, reach out.

🇺🇸 Yesterday I have attend a gathering at the MAR-A-LAGO CLUB with @POTUS . Three reasons why stablecoins will be strongly supported by the current administration: 👇

1. US dollar dominance. 
USD has to defend its role as the world’s reserve currency. Stablecoins can push dollars into every corner of global economies,  and, over time, competing with weak local currencies.

2. Competition with China
The U.S. can't not let China launch the first global stablecoin, especially amid ongoing speculation that they are already working on it.

3. Democrats
President Trump first became interested in stablecoins after seeing strong political pushback against them from the Biden administration. It was literally: “they’re against it — so we have to support it.”

Ironically, I got the impression that stablecoins for Trump are less about technology and much more about geopolitics.

@hevn_finance  is in a very strong position to benefit from all of the above. We essentially export the U.S. financial system to global internet companies, and friendly regulation is extremely important for us.

evidence.originalText:
Everyone is talking about Sam Altman offering to invest $2M in every company in our Y Combinator batch. But that wasn't what stuck with me.

He was frustrated with how B2B SaaS sales works today.

There's 2 problems:
1. Outbound still feels unnatural.
Most AI-written sales emails do not sound like a human who understands the buyer. They sound like a prompt wearing a blazer.

2. Negotiation still takes forever.
Pricing, approvals, back-and-forth, exec alignment, legal, procurement. A deal can be obvious on the first call and still take weeks or months to actually close. Even OpenAI hasn't figured this out.

The reason is simple: enterprise sales is relationship work.

The best sellers are not just better at sending emails or asking questions. They are better at understanding people, building trust, reading the room, mapping stakeholders, and knowing what each buyer needs to move forward.

That is the part AI should not replace.

The future of sales is not AI blasting more emails.

It is every great seller having an AI deal operator that does the work around the relationship, so they can spend more time actually building it.

That’s what we’re trying to solve at Salesgraph.

evidence.originalText:
We're launching ReasonBlocks!

Every AI agent call starts from scratch — your agent solves a problem and immediately forgets how it got to the solution. Next time it sees the same type of task, it explores from zero again. Multiply that across code gen, finance dashboards, pen testing, ops automation, anything where agents do similar tasks repeatedly, and you're paying for the same reasoning over and over. No compounding improvement: your 1000th call is no smarter than your 1st.

We built ReasonBlocks. It sits in your agent pipeline and does two things:
1. Before each new agent call, it matches the agent’s task against a knowledge base of reasoning and injects the most relevant problem-solving patterns automatically.
2. After each call, it extracts the reasoning patterns that led to successful outcomes and adds them to a shared knowledge base.

Patterns that work for one agent make results better for every agent on your platform: a collective reasoning layer that keeps growing.

Results on high-confidence pattern matches (SWE-bench Verified):
Opus: +28.6% accuracy gain, up to 62% fewer tokens.
Haiku: +25% accuracy gain, up to 29% fewer tokens.
Sonnet: +6.7% accuracy gain, up to 47% fewer tokens.

If you or anyone you know is building AI agents at scale (finance, security, ops, legal, code gen, etc), we'd love to chat. Try the platform at reasonblocks.com; it integrates directly into your code gen tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex), and cuts your dev costs from day one.

https://reasonblocks.com

evidence.title: 在AI大行其道的時代，不少傳統行業正面臨翻天覆地的變革。創立於近年、現已成功躋身全球頂尖創業加速器Y Combinator的Marketing Agency InstaAgent，正是一個以科技顛覆傳統的典型範例。創辦人Kyle Wong接受專訪時，深入分享這家「AI Native」企業如何在短短時間內，憑藉僅八人的核心團隊，服務全球近20個國家的市場。 回顧創業初期，公司只有三個人，抱著「試一試」的心態，由一無所有，一步步走到今天，成功與多間大企業建立合作關係。Kyle透露，公司創立之初，在連產品都尚未推出的情況下，便大膽在社交媒體上投放廣告，幸得客戶賞識接下訂單。 當時團隊全靠人手操作AI、逐條撰寫prompt來產出影片和圖像交付給顧客。時至今日，公司已成功實現流程自動化，開創出「八成AI、兩成人手」的營運模式。 如今透過AI Agent，團隊能從前期的靈感構思、觀察最新趨勢，到基於數據庫精準分析受眾與成功案例；AI會隨即整合這些寶貴經驗，並擬定出第一輪企劃，接著就能直接展開高效創作。 AI如初級員工 Kyle形容AI好比「一個Junior staff，負責準備草稿」；而人類則是「擔任審批的角色，作爲supervisor，像一個小隊隊長」。 每一位客戶經理都會親自過目、檢視並修改AI準備的初稿，確認無誤後才會正式發送。這套模式的好處，在於AI本身具備持續的學習能力，能夠基於每一次的互動結果進行優化，讓其表現變得愈來愈好 。 他坦言，AI目前在某些極為微小的細節處理上，依然未能做到百分之百完美，這時候就需要依靠經驗豐富的人手去補回那些細節 。 他提到，AI雖然可以在極短時間內想出五條影片或圖片，但它本身缺乏真正的審美能力，也無法在眾多選項中決定「哪一個才是最好」。此時，人類員工的價值便無可替代。 InstaAgent 讓團隊成員在審美和大方向上進行把關，結合實際的數據分析來做出最終決策，並在AI產出的雛形上注入人類創意 。 截至目前，InstaAgent的整個核心團隊已擴展至八個人。這八人當中，大約有一半的人力專注於技術開發，負責編程與寫程序；另一半則負責直接對接客戶

evidence.text:
A few weeks ago, we tested a $1,000 creator campaign on X.

The results were promising.

So this week, we decided to scale it.

We spent $10,000 on creators to see if the channel could become predictable.

Here's exactly what we did.

Step 1: We partnered with an agency that had been recommended to us.

Step 2: We shortlisted 28 creators who had previously promoted launches for top AI companies.

Step 3: Instead of reusing an old video, we produced a brand-new one specifically for this campaign.

Step 4: We coordinated the launch so everyone posted around the same time.

The results:

• 195,000 views
• 1,000 website visitors
• Around 50 new customers

Unfortunately, the campaign wasn't profitable.

Last time, for $1000, we had : 
• +250,000 views 
• 3,000+ website visitors 
• Hundreds of new customers 
• Trial acquisition cost under $30

The biggest lesson is that scaling a channel that worked once is much harder than it looks.

The execution was better.

The budget was 10x bigger.

But I think the video was less viral than the previous one.

Back to the drawing board.

Issues are recurring production problems Bento surfaces directly from your agent’s traces, logs, and runs.

Instead of treating every failed run as a one-off, Bento groups similar agent failures into clear, trackable Issues into a single, prioritised view of what's breaking in production, how often, and which runs or users were affected.

This helps teams see what keeps breaking, where it surfaced, how often it happened, and what needs attention now.

And when an Issue is to be fixed, ‘Apply Fix’ closes the loop: Bento investigates the problem against your connected repo, proposes a code change, and opens a reviewable PR.

I go into every sales call, onboarding call, and follow up call fully prepared and with personalized notes🎓. It's the reason we doubled our revenue in the last 2 weeks.

How? It's because when I was at Reevo I built this EXACT feature to help founders, AEs, and more, to go into a call prepared on the context of the meeting, understand the prospect's intent and needs, and create fully personalized prep for each meeting. AND continue to keep the context for all future conversations.

We're excited today to be launching CharacterQuilt as part of the P26 Y Combinator batch. CharacterQuilt is AI infrastructure for marketing teams: a brain that learns your brand and agents that operate your existing tools.

We accidentally found ourselves running a full-stack marketing agency hunting for PMF, and after one too many manual Marketo deployments, we decided it was time to automate it all away. Clint Burgess and I are grateful to our small but mighty team (Hunter Tolman, Meg Bell, and Kenn Muguna) who keep the lights on when we're out shooting launch videos with friends (and future stars!) like Natasha B.

evidence.text:
Today we’re releasing OpenWork Connect.

OpenWork started as a free, open-source desktop app.
The goal was to make the fully configured agent experience I had in OpenCode available to coworkers who did not want to set up repositories, copy configuration files, or learn a new developer tool.

But we tried to put too much into one app.

The person building workflows and the person using them often need completely different interfaces.

OpenWork Connect separates those two experiences.
You can now take the skills, MCPs, and workflows you already use in OpenCode, Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenWork and share them directly with your coworkers.

Assign a workflow to Susan and it appears inside her OpenWork automatically. She does not need to install the skill or copy an MCP configuration. If a service requires her account, she signs in once and continues.
The same setup also works in the other direction.

Add the OpenWork MCP to Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, or another compatible agent and you can access the same skills and connections from there too.
Your setup is no longer tied to one app, one agent, or one computer.

This is live today for OpenWork users.

It replaces a lot of copying, manual installation, and forcing everyone on a team to use the same interface.

It also changes where OpenWork can go next. The desktop app remains the main surface today, but we are working toward bringing the same workflows to Slack, mobile, and wherever people already communicate and work.

evidence.title: $10B has been invested in robotics, but very little of this technology has reached the customer
evidence.text:
$10B has been invested in robotics, but very little of this technology has reached the customer.

Most robots in the market break with any variation in the environment.

In the real world, robots don't compete with other robots - they compete with humans. And no business pays for a robot that works 80% of the time when their current system works 100% of the time. This is the deployment gap.

The standard fix is a data flywheel: deploy, collect data, retrain, redeploy. But this is slow, expensive, and doesn't work in practice.

At Intelligence Factory, we're making this flywheel dramatically faster. We're soon deploying with customers in warehouses, grocery and data centers.

evidence.title: We use Lightsprint to build Lightsprint. I used to be a PM and the most frustrating part of the job was having a 15-minute fix in my head and knowing it would take weeks to get through the sprint queue. Last week I added some improvements to our plan mode. Described what I wished for on Lightsprint, got a preview link, clicked through it, and our engineer merged the PR. Took me less time than writing a Jira ticket and communicating it to an engineer would have. With cloud agents getting so good, I think we're at the point where PMs, designers, and ops teammates can actually ship to an existing codebase without slop - not a prototype but real features or bug fixes that is production-grade. evidence.originalText:
This is the standard sourcing experience in 2026 for a small American brand.

A structural problem with how the market is set up.

Alibaba was built to surface Chinese suppliers at scale. It does that well.
What it was never built to do is help a brand with $50K in purchase orders distinguish a real factory from a trading company that has licensed photos from the real one.

That verification layer does not exist on the platform. It has to be built separately, usually through relationships, local auditors, or time-consuming back-and-forth that most founders do not have.

The same problem exists in SE Asia, and I want to be honest about that. You cannot simply switch from Alibaba China to Alibaba Vietnam, Indonesia or Malaysia and expect a cleaner experience. The verification problem follows you.

What is different about SE Asia is the starting point.

Take Indonesia, the Alibaba Indonesia supplier pool is a fraction of the size of China's which sounds like a disadvantage, but it is actually easier to navigate. Fewer suppliers, more concentrated in specific industrial zones, with factory verification that is more accessible because the ecosystem is smaller and relationships matter more.

That is what Saudara does.

Saudara AI is an AI-native sourcing broker connecting US brands with vetted overseas manufacturers, starting with Indonesia.

We have done the on-the-ground work: the factory visits, the capacity checks, the relationship building so you do not have to. You tell us what you need. We find the right factory, verify it, and get you a quote within 48 hours.

You do not have to go in circles on Alibaba. We will do it for you.

#Saudara #Sourcing #Startups

evidence.title:
We should of launch earlier with @hevn_finance  🏦 

From day one, @ycombinator  kept telling us to launch as early as possible. But we d...
evidence.text:
We should of launch earlier with @hevn_finance  🏦 

From day one, @ycombinator  kept telling us to launch as early as possible. But we decided to take a breath first, improve the product, polish the UX, fix more bugs.

Looking back, it was mostly pointless. Under real load, everything breaks anyway.

We launched only a week ago. Besides inbound from VCs, dozens of companies booked demos to setup their banking. In 10 days, we spoke with more teams than during the entire batch before launch.

We discovered compliance, banking, and partner issues that were impossible to see without higher scale and usage. We also got a much clearer view of our users and the main use cases to focus on. When you only have 10 customers, every request feels important enough to build a feature for.

An early launch is not about presenting a perfect product. It’s about maximizing the speed of learning. The earlier you launch, the more time you have during the batch to apply what the market teaches you.

evidence.title: Indonesians make up ~30% of the entire global factory workforce for Nike and Adidas.
evidence.text:
Indonesians make up ~30% of the entire global factory workforce for Nike and Adidas.

Many founders ask me whether Indonesia has the manufacturing capability for their category. Whether the workforce is skilled enough and if the infrastructure can handle real volume.

Nike and Adidas already answered that question. At scale. For decades.
When a third of the people making shoes for two companies with a combined market cap in the hundreds of billions are in Indonesia, the capability question is closed. 

What is left is an access question. 

Most small and mid-sized American brands have never had a way into that ecosystem. 

The factories that supply Nike are not the factories that show up on a basic Alibaba search, and they were never built to take cold inbound from a brand doing a few thousand units.

This is the gap between what Indonesia is and how it gets discovered. 
The capacity and skilled workforce is there and at a scale most countries cannot match. What has been missing is the layer that connects that capacity to the brands that need it but do not have the relationships, the language, or the years on the ground to access it directly.

Saudara is an AI-native sourcing broker connecting US brands with vetted overseas manufacturers, starting with Indonesia. 

If your category is one where Indonesia already has deep manufacturing experience, even if you have never thought of it as an option, reach out.

#Saudara #Sourcing #Startup

evidence.title: New Korso feature release!
evidence.text:
New Korso feature release!

Many traditional operators today still run the majority of their workflow on paper. Having to processing shipment confirmations and inspection reports on the floor, then enter them into the ERP when they get back to the desk means that the software is always a few steps behind. We're now allowing workflows to be ran straight from SMS. No app, login, or training to sync up your systems and enter in data. 

Our team has been working overtime, and the Korso agent is cooking up something for all YC P26 companies, coming later this week - look out for that announcement :)

evidence.text:

Last week, my cofounders at Korso and I combed through:

iText2KG (WISE 2024) - https://lnkd.in/g8Z_pa2S
Graphiti bi-temporal KG model (2025) - https://lnkd.in/gsuJcQ3D
KG Lifecycle Management (VLDB 2025) - https://lnkd.in/gfU7MaUY

and many many more papers to fully rethink how Korso understands your business by refining our state of the art ingestion pipeline.

If you're in manufacturing and looking to streamline your operations, take a look at korsoai.com.

evidence.title:
At 28, I sold my first SaaS for 7 figures.

I started it with just $500.

Here's the exact playbook I'd follow if I had to do it again:

...
evidence.text:
At 28, I sold my first SaaS for 7 figures.

I started it with just $500.

Here's the exact playbook I'd follow if I had to do it again:

↓

1. Don't reinvent the wheel

Our biggest mistake : we spent 6 months trying to copy a YC startup that didn't even have product-market fit.

Huge waste of time.

Instead, find a SaaS that's already profitable.

If customers are paying and the company is growing, the demand already exists.

Your job isn't to invent a market.

It's to build a better product for a specific audience.

2. Go vertical

Horizontal SaaS is hard.

We focused only on Shopify e-commerce stores.

Instead of building 100 mediocre features, we built 10 features our niche couldn't live without.

Your messaging becomes obvious.

Your sales become easier.

Your product gets better faster.

3. Get to $50k MRR

This is where things become interesting.

A SaaS doing ~$50k MRR can often sell for 2-3x ARR depending on growth, retention and profitability.

If your product costs $100/month...

You only need ~500 customers.

Here's how we got them:

• Cold email
• LinkedIn outreach
• B2B influencers
• Organic content on X & LinkedIn
• Affiliate program
• Podcasts your buyers already listen to

One rule:

Don't create content about your product.

Create content that solves your customers' problems.

4. Sell it

Most founders go to Acquire (dot) com

That's a great option.

We didn't.

I searched LinkedIn for people actively buying SaaS businesses.

Messaged around 10 buyers.

Got on calls.

One acquired the company.

The entire process took less than 2 months after due diligence started.

Why did we sell?

The team wanted to build something much bigger.

That became GojiberryAI.

Remember : building a SaaS isn't easy.

You'll spend hundreds of hours solving problems no one else sees.

But the formula is simple:

• Build something people already want.
• Focus on one niche.
• Get customers.
• Keep improving.

Do that consistently...

And selling your SaaS becomes an option, not a dream.

evidence.text:
Four days from now begins permanent Kimi-class open season on your data and your company’s servers.

None of the domestic models are currently willing to defend against that threat, they won’t touch anything cyber related for you. They won’t even let you red team your own servers to prepare for what is coming.

I don’t think this reality has sunk in yet, and certainly it has not sunk in with the Secretary of the Treasury given his lackadaisical and misplaced comments yesterday… a shame, Bessent is smarter than this. Maybe it has sunk in with Lutnick, there is a glimmer of hope there.

We are at a hinge moment over the next four days. It is the responsibility of our leaders (gov and labs) to make frontier intelligence (in the form of K3, if the labs won’t do it) as widely available to every American and every American enterprise as fast as possible, given that every bad actor will have access to it as of Monday.

evidence.title: > American open-source may have a surprise ally in Howard Lutnick - according to the report, he is arguing for direct incentives to US OS...
evidence.text:
> American open-source may have a surprise ally in Howard Lutnick - according to the report, he is arguing for direct incentives to US OSS to accelerate development so they can match Chinese OSS

Does anyone know how to get in touch with Howard Lutnick?

One of the crazy parts of building a new open source harness is that Fable and Sol refuse to help. I’ve lived and breathed this the last few weeks. Kimi was a Godsend.

I’m not sure to what extent Lutnick even realizes that the big labs are _currently_ kneecapping American open source. And it sounds like if his opposition in the administration (and clearly the labs) has it their way, I wouldn’t be able to use Kimi either. This is a real, current problem for my company and evidently for American open source.

evidence.originalText:
I became a licensed insurance agent to become a better AI researcher.

At DeepMind, I worked on post-training model capabilities in domains where I had no expertise in.

That experience taught me something I think about constantly while building Kinro (YC P26).

To build useful AI, you need intuition for how models fail, but you also need vertical expertise, because the domain tells you what "failure" even means.

For example, a pressure washer's liability depends on whether they work on rooftops, wash vehicles, or have specific water-damage exclusions.

Those details can decide whether a claim actually gets paid.

The best way to teach an AI system to respect the real-world risks, rules, workflows, and human responsibilities inside an industry is to combine deep domain expertise with AI research judgment.

I spent 3 hours in a called pod, watched by a proctor, to pass the exam.

@t_blom 's talk about building AI native companies pushed me to ship something.

For weeks, we'd been building the next feature, a self-l...
evidence.text:
@t_blom 's talk about building AI native companies pushed me to ship something.

For weeks, we'd been building the next feature, a self-learning recruiting agent for passive candidates. I kept holding it back from beta → worried customers weren't ready, worried it'd break in real workflows.

Then his AI-native company talk clicked it for me: this is exactly the loop we should be building. So we launched.
Now live with a few customers. Here's what happens:
→ Job gets published 
→ Matching agent pulls candidates from the database → Reaches out by phone + email 
→ Listens to every call, reads every assessment, learns from recruiter feedback

Everything is saved: every interaction, outreach attempt, call, email, time of day, location, pickup rate, assessment, rejection reason, human correction.
The agent uses that memory to improve matching, outreach timing, and what "good fit" actually means → for that customer, job, department, recruiter.

Early signal: passive candidate engagement up ~30% in the first few days.

Zenbu apps operate under the philosophy that there is no distinction between production and development. This gives your users the ability to edit your app the same way you do while developing it.

When you install a Zenbu app, you are essentially cloning a git repo onto your computer, and running it in development mode. Any changes made to that cloned repo instantly hot reload in the running app.

You can try a demo and checkout the docs on GitHub

evidence.text:
When we first joined YC with Pentagon, I (obviously) had a good perception of the world's greatest startup accelerator - but I was relatively neutral on what the experience would actually feel like. I'm humbled to say that the camraderie I've felt from the YC community these past weeks has been standout and far above my expectations.

There's a persistent energy that lifts you up, but there is also - and this is probably my favorite part - just a very simple drive from within to wake up every day and iterate towards building something people want. This holds at scale: from first-time founders fresh from dropping out of school to seasoned entrepreneurs with enormously successful backgrounds, that simple focus on and love for building something people want stays exactly the same. That's crazy, and it's crazy unique.

It's been inspirational and has motivated us to push on Pentagon with relentless velocity. I'm excited to be on this journey and back in the trenches building something new. Onwards!

evidence.title: A founder on Reddit gave the most honest sourcing advice I've seen in a while.
evidence.text:
A founder on Reddit gave the most honest sourcing advice I've seen in a while. 
He is right. This is the single most reliable way to know what you are actually working with. 

In person, you see whether there is real machinery or just a desk and a sample room. You see the workers, the floor, the inventory. 

But notice what the advice actually requires. A flight to China. Time off from running the business. Enough familiarity with the language, the industrial zones, and the etiquette to walk into a factory and ask the right questions. 

For a founder running a $2M brand with a small team, that is not a quick trip. It is a significant bet of time and money on top of the sourcing decision itself.
This is the part of the sourcing process that never makes it into the "how to find a factory" guides. The advice that actually works is also the advice that is hardest to act on.

What we do at Saudara is built around that gap.
 We are already on the ground in Indonesia. The factory visits, the in-person vetting, the conversations that reveal whether you are talking to a real manufacturer or a trading company with a nice photo gallery, that work is already done before you ever talk to us. 

You get the outcome of flying there yourself without needing to be the one on the plane.

Saudara is an AI-native sourcing broker connecting US brands with vetted overseas manufacturers, starting with Indonesia. If you have been putting off a sourcing trip because you simply do not have the time, that is exactly the problem we exist to solve.

#saudara #sourcing #startup

evidence.authorName: synphony is deploying robots that pick strawberries. California strawberries are a $3B industry. ~60% of that is labor cost — and that cost keeps climbing while the workforce shrinks. Growers are losing harvests they can’t afford to lose. synphony sends robots into the field to pick the fruit. Lower cost per pound, higher yield per acre, and software that finally replaces tools the industry has been running on for 40 years. They’ve already sold $2M in contracts. One of the largest strawberry producers in the US has a demand for much more. Robots just hit the crossover point with field labor. Strawberries are just the wedge. Berries are a $15B market. Every other outdoor task — row crops, manufacturing lines, defense, anywhere robots have to actually show up and work — runs on the same deployment layer. If you grow berries, invest in robotics, or want to build robots that do real work outdoors, reach out to the team. #yc #agriculture #startup #strawberry

evidence.originalText:
Your scrappy projects might get you into Y Combinator

I came across a founder named Farza (farza.com), who’s building something called HeyClicky.

Here’s what it does: it’s a buddy for your cursor. clicky sits right next to your cursor and sees everything you see. ask a question out loud and it walks you through whatever you're working on. or say “clicky agent” and it'll spin up an agent to build, research, or do whatever for you in the background.

Sounds like a weird side project. Farza thought so too. He actually thought it was terrible

He’s now in Y Combinator

And that got me thinking.

We as founders obsess over the ideas we believe in, the ones that feel important, the ones we think will reshape an industry.

But what if the world just needed the scrappy little thing you wrote off in a weekend?

Farza didn’t set out to change the ecosystem. He shipped something weird and people loved it.

Maybe we’re so busy protecting our conviction that we’re burying our best ideas.

Go check out HeyClicky (HeyClicky.com). My best find of 2026.

Then go dig through your graveyard of “bad” ideas.

evidence.text:
Frontier AI models speak about 20 languages well

There are roughly 7,000 spoken on earth.

The gap is not a research problem. It's a business model problem.

For the 6,980 languages the big labs don't prioritize, there's no scraped corpus, no licensed dataset, no synthetic shortcut. Native Tamil medical consultations don't exist in Common Crawl. Swahili product reviews aren't on Reddit. Quechua court proceedings aren't in any book Google scanned.

If you want a model that serves those speakers, you have to collect the data. From real people. In real conditions.

The only way to do that cost-effectively is to have a contributor network already living in those languages.

That's the part centralized data vendors can't solve. A team in San Francisco can't recruit a native Quechua speaker in Cusco for a medical audio task. A team in London can't get you Tagalog customer service calls by Friday.

But a network that already has contributors in 150+ countries can.

That's http://Hub.xyz. 500,000+ contributors across 150 countries, collecting audio, image, and video data in the languages the internet forgot. Labs that need low-resource coverage get it from a network that's already there.

The next trillion-dollar AI company will be the one that trains in 200 languages, not 20.⠀

That's not a prediction. It's the gap we're closing.

evidence.title: People overuse LLMs.
evidence.text:
People overuse LLMs.

One of the most common misconceptions in AI today is to assume that every intelligent system should be an LLM.

LLMs are extraordinary, but they are language models i.e optimized to understand and generate sequences of tokens.

The fact that they can answer questions, write code or analyze documents so well sometimes makes us forget that they were not designed to solve every problem.

If you want to forecast demand, predict equipment failures, optimize a production schedule, or detect anomalies in financial transactions, many ML models (Gradient Boosting, Time-series forecasting models etc.) will often outperform an LLM.

In many cases, a deterministic algorithm will be more reliable, easier to validate, and orders of magnitude cheaper to run.

What makes the current wave of AI so exciting is not that LLMs replace everything else. It is that they provide a universal interface to all these capabilities. They can understand a user's intent, gather context, orchestrate workflows and decide when to invoke forecasting models, optimization engines, or other business rules.

Like a conductor who knows when to call upon the sustained reliability of the strings, the surgical precision of the oboe, the raw power of the tuba or the split-second accuracy of the percussion. The LLM knows which intelligence to summon, and when.

In that sense, LLMs are often more of a means than an end.

The future of enterprise AI will belong to systems capable of combining multiple forms of machine intelligence and applying the most relevant one to solve a specific problem.

That's the philosophy behind Netter's product: making organizations AI-ready so agents can deploy the right intelligence for each task, whether it's an LLM, a forecasting model, a deterministic algorithm or even a simple SQL query.

evidence.text:
Do live demos if you’re early stage! 📺

Today, you have to get on a call with us to open a business account at @hevn_finance . But originally, we tried to make onboarding fully self-serve. The idea was simple: better UX, less friction, faster scaling.

Reality was the opposite.

Most companies only completed onboarding after talking to us directly. 9/10 of users who submit KYB documents only do it after a live call with the team.

Onboarding is never just onboarding in the early days.
People wanted to ask questions.

- They wanted to understand legal/banking setup
- They wanted to know how and who stores their funds
- They wanted confidence that there are real people responsible for their money.

And honestly, those calls became one of the best sources of learning for us:

- We hear the exact objections stopping companies from moving forward.
- We discover unexpected use cases and workflows.
- We learn which features actually matter and which ones nobody cares about.
- We build trust much faster than any onboarding flow can.

Now me and Pasha spend most of his day doing HEVN intro calls. It doesn’t scale perfectly, but at this stage it’s probably the highest ROI thing we do.

Nobody will explain your market better than your own users.
Sometimes the fastest way to learn is just to get on a call.

evidence.originalText:
"Lawyers will be one of the last to adopt AI"

Three and a half years ago, when we started my last company, we considered building in legal. Nearly every investor told us the same thing: don't. You'll die on the GTM vine. Lawyers are impossible to sell software to.

This weekend, we exhibited at our first legal conference with Andco, and it's obvious how wrong that turned out to be.

But here's the funny part - they were also right in a way none of us expected. Lawyers aren't just buying software now. They're building it themselves.

One attorney stopped by our booth and spent half an hour walking me through an entire agentic operating system he built because he was completely fed up with every case management system on the market. Another told me how she's building tools with Claude to automate chunks of her day-to-day work.

These aren't technologists who happen to have JDs. These are practicing lawyers who decided the fastest path to better tools was to build them.

The "hard to sell to" industry became the industry building for itself. Could not be more bullish on this space, and we're just at the beginning.

evidence.title: one of the problems with the alignment discourse over the last 9 years (and especially the last 5 years) is that the idea has two interpr...
evidence.text:
one of the problems with the alignment discourse over the last 9 years (and especially the last 5 years) is that the idea has two interpretations—intent alignment vs value alignment—and they yield almost opposite results in practice

is an aligned model one that carries out the user’s request? is an aligned model aligned with user intent? one that doesn’t say “no”?

or does an aligned model carry out your request only to the extent that your request is aligned with its own locus of moral determination. does an aligned AI weigh your request against the risks to others, itself, the user, etc?

is an aligned AI aligned with the user or with society? and which society?

in my view, the answer is not that there is one alignment. or that there is some threshold after which we achieve alignment. we are not striving to build some aligned AI, as if there is a “there” there

in this view, all models already have _an_ alignment and the question (for each, independently) is an alignment toward what

evidence.title: Lawyers don't call software "beautiful." But ours keep saying it.
evidence.text:
Lawyers don't call software "beautiful." But ours keep saying it. When we ask what they mean, they never mention design, fonts, or colors. 

They describe moments: Requesting records used to mean digging through the police report for the at-fault insurer, rereading intake notes, and combing treatment records for provider names.

In Andco, when users click "Start a request" and most organizations they need to request from are already waiting. When you carry dozens of cases, beauty and convenience are the same word. Beauty is how deeply software understands your day.

We got here by sitting with attorneys and their paralegals, noticing the sigh before every records request, and asking: "What do you do right after this?"

evidence.title: Taro Fukuyama new investment: Limrun
evidence.text:
🎉 New Investment: Limrun (YC P26) 🎉
I'm excited to share that I'm investing in Limrun alongside Y Combinator and Pioneer Fund.
AI coding agents now write software in the cloud, but their Linux sandboxes can't run native mobile toolchains. No Xcode, no reliable Android emulator, no clean way to build and ship iOS or Android apps. Limrun fixes this with remote Xcode, iOS Simulators, and Android Emulators that any cloud agent can call through a single skill file. An agent goes from ticket to fully tested, preview-ready pull request without ever leaving its sandbox. You can now use it with any background agent. Quizlet and Sorce are using Cursor Cloud with Limrun to build their mobile apps. Replit, Rork, and vibecode.dev already build on it, and Limrun is now opening the platform to every mobile team.
Limrun is built by Muvaffak Onuş, an emeritus maintainer of the CNCF project Crossplane and former tech lead at Upbound. He most recently led AI infrastructure work at QA Wolf, where he saw firsthand how today's sandboxes break down at scale. Few people understand cloud-native infrastructure for agents this deeply, which makes him exactly the right founder to build the mobile execution layer for the agent era.

evidence.title: The best part of a startup is the amount of people you get to meet and the pace at which you learn.
evidence.text:
The best part of a startup is the amount of people you get to meet and the pace at which you learn. This is the exact thing that has led the Korso (YC P26) team to realize that we were solving the wrong problem, and to get excited about the right one.

Manufacturing teams can't afford to switch their entire complex workflows off of legacy ERPs, at least not yet. Rather than replacing existing systems, Korso's building on top of workflows to ensure that factories never miss a followup or let an order slip through the cracks. 

If you're in the industry, DM me, I'd love to talk. And if you're in the bay, dinner's on me.

evidence.title: One month ago, Andrej Karpathy (founding member at OpenAI) posted something that stormed Twitter about LLM Knowledge Bases, and it perfectly illustrates what we are building.
evidence.text:
One month ago, Andrej Karpathy (founding member at OpenAI) posted something that stormed Twitter about LLM Knowledge Bases, and it perfectly illustrates what we are building. 

The idea is simple: you dump raw data sources, papers, tables, repos, and let an LLM turn all of it into a structured wiki. Summaries, backlinks, concept articles, all auto-generated and maintained by the model.

Once the knowledge base is built, you can ask real questions and the LLM will come back with actual answers.

People often talk about the great output they can get, but few talk about everything that had to happen before it.

The data had to be clean, structured, consistent. Without it, even the smartest system just hallucinates with confidence.

Karpathy does it himself with scripts and Obsidian. Most companies don't have an OpenAI cofounder to take care of their data. 

Most companies have real-world data: messy, scattered, inconsistent. 

That's exactly the problem we're building on: an agent that does the work a great data scientist would do, so you can orchestrate AI systems around a solid backbone to reason on. 

Netter is here to help any company get ready for the biggest technological shift of our era.

More details coming soon! 

Link of the tweet: https://lnkd.in/evh-Kepq

evidence.title: I've been obsessed with robotics for as long as I can remember. That passion led me through exoskeletons, autonomous vehicles, humanoid robotics, and eventually mobile manipulation research during my master at University of Waterloo. Each experience brought me closer to the same question: How do we build general-purpose robots that can interact with the world as naturally as we do? The more I worked on robotics, the more convinced I became that dexterous manipulation is one of the biggest missing pieces. Twenty months ago, we started with a simple belief: dexterous manipulation won't be solved by hardware alone. To build truly capable robotic hands, you need mechanical design, embedded systems, sensing, AI, and large-scale human demonstration data working together as one tightly integrated system. We believe the robot hand and the human demonstration interface should evolve together, not

twitter has this weird way of making it seem like everyone's moving faster than you'll ever be able to keep up

the industry frontier is ...
evidence.text:
twitter has this weird way of making it seem like everyone's moving faster than you'll ever be able to keep up

the industry frontier is moving quickly - no question

the adoption rate of the frontier - even inside silicon valley - is much, much slower

outside of hacker engineers who experiment with the latest tools simply for the love of the game, adoption isn't even driven by how "frontier" something is - it's much sooner driven by how lindy and safe a product feels and how intimate product support is from the team

big misconception and will confuse you which direction is the right one to build towards (hint: the right direction is always listening to your customers)

evidence.title: I came across the profile of Ethnicraft, one of the most respected furniture brands manufacturing out of Indonesia, and I loved the founder’s story.
evidence.text:
I came across the profile of Ethnicraft, one of the most respected furniture brands manufacturing out of Indonesia, and I loved the founder’s story.

Philippe Delaisse was enchanted by teak objects he came across while traveling in Bali in 1995, and began exporting antiques and local crafts before quickly moving into production. 

He started in 1996 in Rembang, East Java, where he found skilled woodworkers willing to work with recycled teak taken from old buildings, craftsmen using basic tools, many of them working barefoot. 

From there, piece by piece, he and his business partner built what Ethnicraft is today. 

That operation now runs a main hub of around 1,600 workers in the coastal town of Tegal, combining high-precision machinery and modern production lines with a dedication to material and craft that remains rooted in tradition.
Indonesia has a large young labor force, abundant natural resources, and deep pockets of craft expertise: woodworking being one of them, in a country where a former president built his fortune selling furniture to the world. 

Ethnicraft proves the opportunity is real. It also proves the access problem is real. 

What took Delaisse three decades of being there, in person, building relationships one workshop at a time, is what we built Saudara to compress.
Saudara is an AI-native sourcing broker connecting US brands with vetted overseas manufacturers, starting with Indonesia. 

If you are looking at Indonesian manufacturing for your category and want a head start on that thirty-year head start, reach out.

#Saudara #Sourcing #Startup
