evidence.originalText:
The AI Engineer World’s Fair had 100s of the same booths:

AI SREs that takes a bug alert to PR from Slack.

It’s great low hanging fruit. But it’s not what most companies need the most.

We started Runtime on a bet: coding agents can do a lot more than ship software for the sake of software development.

At Runtime (YC P26), we see software as a means to an end.

A support team wires an agent into their stack, Zendesk, Pylon, whatever they run. If gluing those together means writing some code, it writes it. Nobody on that team cares about the code. They care about closing tickets faster and hitting SLA.

A marketing team that needs rapid landing page and blog post iteration does the same. They have an agent that changes their website and ships experiments to accomplish higher conversion rates without needing to wait on the eng team.

That’s where our obsession lives.

If you’re using coding agents outside of engineering, what has been the most useful use cases?

evidence.title: Atrisa (YC P26) is building Atrisa - Agents for Analog Circuit Design. Analog Circuit Design relies heavily on experience and intuition, making it difficult for AI to enable increases in productivity - until now. Atrisa enables tokenmaxxing for Analog Circuit Engineers. It hierarchically reasons about your circuit, finds the right topologies to match your specifications, and does deep-dive debugging and experimentation. It takes into context everything an analog engineer would need: Reusability across older designs, possible interference, parasitics, physical layout context. It can talk to other instances, so you don't get blocked by another engineers availability. Along with providing a modern chat based interface, Atrisa fits seamlessly in your existing workflows. evidence.title: Every Andco customer gets a full client platform included.
evidence.text:
Every Andco customer gets a full client platform included. Here's why we built it.

We kept hearing the same thing from firms: it's hard to get documents from your own client. Weeks of follow-up for something that takes two minutes.

And on the other end of the line, the client is going through the worst stretch of their year. They're hurt, out of work, and anxious. So they call, email, and text to ask where the case stands. Did the medical records come in? The police report? The insurance response? The silence in between is the hardest part.

That part of the workflow needed to be reinvented, not patched.

Most client portals in legal feel like an afterthought. Ours is a full-fledged product. Clean and fast, built for the phone in their pocket, the kind of experience people expect from the apps they use every day, not from a law firm. Clients upload documents and sign forms in a few taps. Or they link their records with us directly through major hospital systems, no paperwork at all. And they can see where their case stands without having to ask.

Everything lands in the case file automatically.

If you're evaluating Andco, you're not just buying agents for records retrieval and insurance verification. You're buying a better experience for people who badly need one. That's the client experience.

evidence.text: Today we moved Kimpton AI to consumption-based pricing for individuals and emerging managers. Seat-based software priced access. That worked when software just sat there waiting to be operated. Agents change it. evidence.title: Napkin Math (YC P26) is the hyper-personalized AI food journal that helps people achieve their health goals. Existing consumer health apps focus on scaling a one-size-fits-all solution: calorie deficits. But they don’t answer the questions you actually have. Napkin Math tailors a plan for not only your specific health goal, but also your life. Before AI, personalization was impossible. Tailoring a plan to every chronic condition, allergy, goal, and stage of life was impossible. With frontier models, we’re able to reimagine nutrition experiences from the ground up. Napkin Math understands how to make taking a picture of your food fun. How come Instagram foodies, who religiously follow “the camera eats first”, don’t also log their food in a journal? Napkin Math perfectly marries the joy of socially sharing your food with a rich database that can help foodies feel better every day. The team

evidence.originalText:
Teleoperation is moving out of the lab and into real factories- and last week at iREX Tokyo, we got to showcase what that looks like 🇯🇵🤖.

Avea Robotics demoed our real-time, low-latency humanoid teleoperation with our integration partner TRON K.K. Attendees on the floor got a chance to see how operators can control their robots with precision and reliability⚡️.

Moments like this highlight why we’re so focused on bridging the gap between incredible robotic hardware and practical, real-world deployment. Teleoperation is becoming a key enabler for bringing robots out of the lab and into daily operations, and it was exciting to see how many manufacturers and integrators are ready for solutions they can adopt today.

Huge thank you to kei wajima and the entire TRON team for hosting us! Looking forward to what we build together next 🙌.

#robotics #teleoperation #irex2025 #manufacturing #startups

Saudara AI (YC P26) is an AI broker connecting American brands with the world's best factories. We sell outcomes, not software. A real broker on every deal, supercharged by AI to move 10x faster at a fraction of the cost of a traditional sourcing agent.

Every year, brands lose billions sourcing overseas. Hidden fees, ghost suppliers, wrong specs, missed deadlines. The best factories sit behind decades-old relationships that most Western buyers can't access. We have those relationships. Our AI handles the rest.

Built by a third-generation manufacturer and an Amazon supply chain veteran, two people who've spent their careers on both sides of this problem.

Founders:
Edward Haryono — Co-founder & CEO. Amazon supply chain background. President of IABA-PNW (Promoting Indonesian & Pacific Northwest Trade)
Jennifer Prasetyo — Co-founder & CTO. Third-generation Indonesian manufacturer. Creator behind @jenandtech.

evidence.originalText:
11:07 p.m. is a terrible time to discover your demo has no story.

That is the moment I keep seeing technical teams hit.

The product is solid. The release is almost ready. Someone is trying to record a narrated walkthrough while three other people are rewriting a Hacker News title in a doc.

None of this work is glamorous.

But it is the surface area where a release becomes legible.

A demo needs to show the right path, not every menu. Hacker News needs plain language, not a launch poster. Social needs to sound like the founder, not like product notes got pasted into AI.

That is why Memoir prepares launch-ready assets as part of the growth system.

It turns the raw material around a release into narrated demo videos, Hacker News-specific prep, and founder-voice posts that are ready to be polished instead of started from scratch.

The point is not to make more content.

The point is to protect the moment when a shipping team finally has attention pointed at it.

Because when technical teams do this well, the work does not need to be translated by a marketing department months later.

The product can explain itself while the team keeps building.

evidence.originalText:
10 weeks at Y Combinator and one marketer's story yesterday tied the whole thing together for me.

The marketer was in Ops and is really leaning into AI. He built a full engine for producing blog content, from keyword research, to external research, pulling in positioning/trends, etc.

But it all stopped at getting it live in the CMS. He can't get the last 10% to work. Why?

He said it was because they host all their visual content in a CDN. To publish it, someone has to:
1-) Find an image
2-) Upload to CDN
3-) Grab the specific CDN embed link
4-) Embed that link into the CMS.

He called it "layers of complexity and nuance that I haven't even tried to figure out how to build into my workflow."

This "last 10%" is killing marketers right now.

Everyone posts about the AI that gets them 90% of the way there. Then it hits a CDN, a CMS, a Figma file, etc. etc.

The last 10% is real engineering to stitch this together. (ok, i had to...CharacterQuilt after all 🧵 )

It's been such a cool thing to see marketers get unstuck when they have some eng infrastructure underneath them.

evidence.title: A YC founder asked Eric Ries: is scale inherently corrupting? His answer: scale is a form of pressure. And pressure reveals the blueprint a company was built on. Ries told the story of Sol Price, who built Price Club on two principles: low prices and high wages. When the company went public, investors pushed him out. They looked at what he'd built and saw warehouses to squeeze. He saw an engine of interlocking principles you couldn't touch without breaking the whole thing. Seven years later, they liquidated the company. Sol Price took those same principles, and they became the foundation for Costco Wholesale. Same founder, same ideas, completely different outcome. Costco built structural protection around its founding ethos. Price Club left it exposed. Ries calls this force "financial gravity." Every company that succeeds will feel it. The question is what you've built to withstand it. I

evidence.title: One of the hardest tensions in early-stage building is speed vs.
evidence.text:
One of the hardest tensions in early-stage building is speed vs. scope.

Every week at Andco, there's a pull to build the ocean. We talk to new law firms and get requests for every workflow a plaintiff firm could ever want - records, bills, liens, claims, seo, marketing, all of it.

That vision is right. It's definitely where we're headed. But it's not what wins.

What wins is shipping absolute killer features. The one thing that makes a managing partner stop mid-demo and say "wait, that's all we have to do?" The feature that saves a case manager 8+ hours on a single file. That's what gets us in the door, gets us referred, and gets us renewed.

So we've been forcing ourselves into a discipline here early on: ship the sharp thing first. Let the platform emerge from a stack of features firms cannot imagine living without.

evidence.originalText:
The worst time to write a founder post is usually the moment you finally have something worth saying.

A customer call ends. There is one sentence in the transcript that explains the product better than your homepage.

A metric moved. Not enough for a press release. Definitely enough for a useful post.

A product update went out. The team understands why it matters because they lived inside the work for weeks. Everyone else just sees another vague announcement.

This is the gap technical teams keep falling into.

The signal exists. The proof exists. The timing exists.

But turning it into credible content still means someone has to stop building, remember the context, pull the thread together, and write in a voice that does not sound like a committee discovered adjectives.

Memoir’s founder-voice content generation is built for that exact moment.

It takes product updates, customer signals, current events, and tracked metrics, then turns them into posts for LinkedIn, X, Hacker News, and blogs that sound like the founder actually wrote them.

Not as a sales pitch.

As anchored attribution. Proof tied to the thing the team actually did, said in the language the market already understands.

For engineering-led teams, this matters because attention should not depend on whether the founder had two spare hours and a clean Google Doc.

The future I care about is one where every shipping team has a credible distribution loop running alongside the product loop.

Where useful work does not disappear because nobody had the energy to package it.

evidence.title: Você trocaria o carro ou a moto pela bike no seu dia a dia? E se pagassem para você fazer isso? Estamos felizes em anunciar as inscrições abertas para o 2º piloto do Programa Bike SP, um projeto do IME-USP e do FGV Cidades em parceria com a SMT e a SPTrans, da Prefeitura de São Paulo. A ideia é simples e cientificamente rigorosa: testar se pagar créditos no Bilhete Único por quilômetro pedalado é capaz de mudar de verdade os hábitos de mobilidade em São Paulo. Os resultados vão ajudar a prefeitura a desenhar, com base em evidências, a política pública definitiva do programa. Estamos especialmente interessados em participantes que ainda pedalam pouco ou não pedalam em seus deslocamentos diários. Se esse é o seu caso, esse é o momento ideal para experimentar: você ganha créditos de transporte público só por trocar alguns trajetos de carro ou moto pela bicicleta. Requisitos: ser maior de id

evidence.originalText:
We are building socially intelligent humanoid robots for caregiving.

Our semi-humanoids go into nursing homes, senior living communities, and care facilities to support elderly residents. They handle daily tasks like feeding, dressing, medication, and object retrieval, while providing genuine social and emotional companionship. We build the full stack in-house: the robot hardware and all the AI that makes it socially capable, so one caregiver can do more for more residents in a field facing chronic staffing shortages.
While the rest of robotics chases object manipulation like moving boxes and folding laundry, we're focused on the harder, more meaningful problem: how people and robots work together.

This is our founder launch. If caregiving is one of the most important problems of the next decade, we want to build with the people who see it that way too.

evidence.authorName: The AI wave is what everyone is talking about.
evidence.title: The AI wave is what everyone is talking about.
evidence.text: The AI wave is what everyone is talking about. evidence.title: I agree, transformer models natively have no way to evaluate confidence so every answer is always 100% confident and that's the nature of...
evidence.text:
I agree, transformer models natively have no way to evaluate confidence so every answer is always 100% confident and that's the nature of the architecture.

For example in document AI, you would want a dedicated OCR model that can generate confidence scores and bounding boxes but then use that as Evidence grounding. This improves accuracy significantly but still far from perfect since the transformer is still the final model. We benchmarked this here: https://interfaze.ai/leaderboards/structured-output-benchmark

This is why we had to design Interfaze which is a Mixture of Architecture for specialized use cases

evidence.originalText:
The EU just agreed to make product compliance "digital by default" across the Single Market.

Everyone read it as "less paperwork."

That's not the story. The real shift is from compliance as documents to compliance as data.

A Declaration of Conformity you can auto-generate, serve by QR code, and keep current isn't a document anymore, it's a view onto data sitting underneath it.

Which raises the only question that matters: is your compliance data actually structured, current, and ready to be served on demand?

For most companies, it isn't. It lives in drives, inboxes, supplier emails and spreadsheets, a binder-era setup for a digital-first world.

The EU just made data the unit that counts.

evidence.title: Analog chips are crucial and complex. Yet, it’s a corner of chip design AI-for-EDA hasn’t cracked yet. I spoke with Rithik Jain, co-founder of Atrisa (YC P26), on building agentic AI for analog circuit design. Highlights: 1️⃣ Analog resists automation. Digital has clean abstraction layers but in analog, components couple (parasitics, interference etc). Human intuition matters. 2️⃣ Atrisa's bet: rent intelligence (frontier models), own intuition (Atrisa’s multi-agent architecture, tuned with RLVR) 3️⃣ Analog suits RLVR. SPICE is a fast, faithful verifier. Without binary pass/fail, designs get scored on a continuum across competing constraints (weights set during training). 4️⃣ Analog training data is sparse. Atrisa built a custom dataset of ~2000 circuits and converted a data problem into an architecture problem. 5️⃣ With agentic chip design, per-seat pricing will likely give way to a hyb

evidence.originalText:
Every frontier model tested capped under 80% accuracy on a real financial task. One smaller model reached 84.7%

The study comes from Bridgewater and Thinking Machines Lab. GPT, Claude, and Gemini all hit the same ceiling, and newer generations barely moved the number: GPT 5.4 costs 43% more than 5.2 for a marginal gain.

Then a smaller, open-weight model, fine-tuned on data that real investment experts labeled instead of a generic vendor, reached 84.7% accuracy. 29.8% fewer errors than the best frontier model, at 13.8x lower cost.

Swap "financial judgment" for almost any task that depends on real human expertise or lived experience, and the finding holds.

This is why Hub exists. The data that actually moves model performance is rarely the data that is easiest to scrape or cheapest to label. It is the data only a real expert, or a real person living the experience, can provide.

#AI #DataInfrastructure #EnterpriseAI #MachineLearning #FutureOfWork

evidence.originalText:
We watched a shopper spend 11 minutes on a product page for a pair of trail shoes.

She asked nothing. Clicked nothing. Left.

We pulled the session recording afterward. She had scrolled past the weight specs, the lug depth breakdown, the "as worn by elite athletes" badge.

None of it was wrong. None of it was for her.

She was buying a birthday gift for her husband. She wanted to know if they'd arrive in time and whether she could return them if the size was off.

The page never told her.

That moment stuck with us. Because the store had done everything right by conventional standards. Good photography. Strong copy. Social proof. Fast load time.

But there was one version of that page. And it was written for someone else.

That's the thing about ecommerce that most people don't say out loud:

Every shopper who lands on your product page is a different person with a different reason to buy.

The runner wants pace and drop and stack height.

The gift buyer wants shipping windows and return policies.

The first-time buyer wants reassurance.

The repeat customer wants to skip everything they already know.

One static page cannot do that job for all four of them.

So we built Kinect around a simple premise.

The store stays exactly as it is. The experience changes based on who's browsing and why.

A shopping assistant answers the questions your page can't anticipate. The product page itself adapts its content and messaging based on the shopper's context.

And the intelligence dashboard tells you, after the fact, what people were actually asking, what made them convert, and what made them leave.

That woman who spent 11 minutes and left? She told us everything we needed to know.

We just had to build something that could listen.

evidence.authorName: Production replica of any repo in seconds.
evidence.title: Production replica of any repo in seconds.
evidence.text: Production replica of any repo in seconds. No Docker or terraform. Just Claude Code. Import a repo in Runtime, we spin up a sandbox with Claude Code and snapshot it: dependencies installed, secrets injected, and servers running. Every session after starts from that snapshot. This used to take me days to set up per repo for each customer. Custom scripts, Docker, manual dependency installs. Multiply that across customers and it was our biggest onboarding bottleneck. Now it's self-serve. And this also allow us to dogfood Runtime inside Runtime. Go give it a try!
evidence.originalText:
Production replica of any repo in seconds.

No Docker or terraform. Just Claude Code.

Import a repo in Runtime, we spin up a sandbox with Claude Code and snapshot it: dependencies installed, secrets injected, and servers running. 

Every session after starts from that snapshot. 

This used to take me days to set up per repo for each customer. 

Custom scripts, Docker, manual dependency installs. 

Multiply that across customers and it was our biggest onboarding bottleneck.

evidence.text:
If you’ve ever had an entire workflow break because a borrower updated their accounting software and renamed a spreadsheet column from Inv_Date to Billing_Date, you already know how brittle traditional automation is.

Everyone keeps saying "just use AI." or "give it to claude"

But the reality is that an AI error isn't just an awkward typo in a marketing email. It’s an undetected cross-aging dilution, a corrupted ineligible calculation, or an over-advance that vaporizes your collateral cushion.

The truth? AI is an incredible precision tool, but dropping it into a 30-year-old core system without customized data engineering, ontop of processes that are discretional to each employee, not knowing what to ask or what to expect is an existential risk to your capital and your reputation.

We do believe that AI can make your operations run smoother, but we know it's not just waving the magic wand.

Join Isa, Zolvo's CEO for a beginner friendly technical briefing designed exclusively for senior lenders. 

Expect to end the session knowing the basics of how to implement AI, what to expect from implementation and how to avoid common mistakes.

Save your spot here: https://luma.com/giuei6jj

evidence.originalText:
One of the biggest misconceptions we hear from new DME suppliers is that commercial enrollment should be straightforward after Medicare enrollment is complete.

Unfortunately, that's rarely the case.

Although Medicare is a proofpoint, commercial enrollment is an entirely different process.

Each payer has its own contracting requirements, timeline, documentation, and network strategy. While some large commercial carriers offer nationwide DME contracts, most still require state-by-state enrollment (BCBS). In addition to understanding which intermediary organizations are required for certain payers (think Optum for UnitedHealthCare), this creates a hurdle for DME suppliers looking to serve a nationwide patient base.

After speaking with DME suppliers across the country, we've noticed the same themes come up again and again:
• How long should enrollment actually take?
• Why does BCBS require separate contracts by state?
• What are organizations like CareCentrix and Optum, and when do they matter?
• Should I continue billing out-of-network while I wait?

We put together a practical guide that answers these questions and walks through the commercial enrollment process step by step.

If you're a DME supplier expanding beyond Medicare, we hope it's helpful.

evidence.authorName: Look at the windows. Every one of them is lit. Every one of them is a person teaching a machine to do something your body already knows by heart. Third floor. A woman folds laundry, her hands moving the way yours do, without thinking. Smoothing the towel flat. Finding the corners. She isn't filming her face. She's filming her hands. Two floors down someone fills the sink until it steams and starts on the dishes, one plate at a time. Down the hall a bed gets made. On a sill above, a watering can tips over the plants and the soil goes dark. Your body knows every one of these motions. A machine knows none of them. That's the whole reason these windows are lit tonight. Every gesture so worn-in you forgot you ever learned it is exactly what robots can't do and can't find anywhere online, because nobody thought to record it. Hub records it. Four dollars an hour of first-person video. For a lot of people behind this glass, that's more than a day's wage, earned doing things they'd be doing anyway. São Paulo. Bogotá. Buenos Aires. One building of unremarkable evenings, in the cities the industry keeps forgetting to look at. This is the other side of AI. Not the lab. The life behind the windows. The door downstairs is open. Someone's already walking in.

evidence.title: It’s such a cool idea. The SSU had already tried a few times to hit strategic bomber aircraft like the Tu-95 using more 'standard', long-range drones - but it was difficult. S-400 missile system have become better at defending against such attacks. And more importantly, the standard radar systems at those locations are very effective at detecting mid-sized drones in the sky, giving plenty of time to prepare. I'd bet the original idea at SSU started with a seemingly dumb question like: "Can we use FPV drones to strike?" Someone probably replied, "No, it’s over 4000km away." And that’s when the Aha moment happened. Then came the brainstorming: how do we secretly deploy a massive number of drones near all the airbases - because you can't repeat the same operation twice. Genius hacking mindset! And such a carefully executed operation - it stayed hidden for 18 months! …more

evidence.title: Genuinely think hiring devops in 2026 slows the whole team down. 10 minutes to spin up a VM before the environment can run a single thing...
evidence.text:
Genuinely think hiring devops in 2026 slows the whole team down. 10 minutes to spin up a VM before the environment can run a single thing, that too on a good day. Not to mention it adds up with a compound interest as it gets handed down. every good engineer I know spends more time fighting their setup than actually building something.

and I’m pretty sure I speak for most engineers here: You sit down, ready to work, and out of nowhere you’re 30 tabs deep figuring out why the environment that ran fine on friday is throwing errors on monday. Nobody touched it, but it feels a lot like a doom you can’t escape.

And when they finally fix it? Nobody knows how, and you definitely don’t breathe in its general direction lol.

Isn’t it wild to think that THESE people are the some of the smartest in their job, and they are spending their best hours babysitting infra that resents them?

evidence.originalText:
When someone gets hurt, the system that's supposed to help them moves at the speed of a fax machine. Records requests sit for weeks. Police reports get mailed. Insurance verifications bounce between adjusters and paralegals. The person who was actually injured waits, often while bills pile up and the insurance company's first lowball offer starts to look tempting.

Plaintiff-side law firms didn't choose this. They inherited it. The best firms in the country still run intake on spreadsheets and staff rooms full of people whose job is to call hospitals on hold. A case that should take three weeks to work up takes four months. Firms turn away cases they'd win because they can't staff the paperwork. Injured people get less, later.

We think the pre-litigation phase is where plaintiff work actually lives or dies. It's where you learn whether a case is real, what it's worth, and whether your client gets a fair shot. Automating it isn't a back-office upgrade. It's the difference between a firm overwhelmed by volume, turning away cases it would win, and a future where everyone who deserves representation gets it.

Andco chases the paper so law firms can chase justice for more clients. Medical records, police reports, insurance verifications, demand drafts, all handled by agents. More cases taken. More people made whole. That's Andco. Accelerating justice.

evidence.title: We never thought we'd compare Zolvo to a referee.
evidence.text:
We never thought we'd compare Zolvo to a referee. But here we are.

Think about VAR for a second.

The referee runs the whole match. Makes the call. Keeps things moving.
VAR only gets checked when something looks wrong.

That's exactly how Zolvo works for accounting teams.

Every reconciliation. Every debtor pool update. Every NOA. Every transaction running quietly in the background.

Zolvo makes the call. In real time. No human needed to babysit it.

Your accounting team doesn't touch it (they don't have to).

They only step in when something's actually exceptional. A mismatch. A flag. Something that needs a real human decision.

That's it. That's the whole job now.

Not reviewing 100% of transactions like it's still 2015.
Just reviewing the 2% that actually matter.

We built this because we watched teams manually checking EVERY play when they should've been trusting the system and only stepping in for the controversial calls.

The best referees are invisible. You only notice them when something's wrong.

That's the product we're building.

evidence.originalText:
Your best marketing asset is probably sitting in a customer call no one has time to rewatch.

A technical team ships something useful.

The customer reaction is buried in a transcript. The metric that proves it mattered is sitting in a dashboard. The founder has the right take, but it came out sideways on a call between three other meetings.

Then someone opens a blank doc and tries to turn all of that into a post.

That is where most credible content gets flattened.

Not because the team has nothing to say. Because the signal is scattered, and the person who understands the product is usually the person least available to package it.

This is one of the core jobs Memoir does.

It turns product updates, customer signals, current events, and tracked metrics into founder-voice content for the places technical buyers actually read. LinkedIn. X. Blogs. Hacker News-style posts when the topic deserves that room.

The important part is not “AI writes posts.” That framing is too small.

The important part is that a shipping team can stop treating distribution like a separate creative ritual that starts from a blank page.

A useful moment happens. Memoir catches the proof around it. The draft shows up in the founder’s voice, anchored in what actually happened, not polished into generic SaaS fog.

That changes the rhythm.

Content becomes a byproduct of real product motion. Proof, never as a sales pitch.

The teams that win attention over the next few years will not be the loudest ones. They will be the ones that turn every meaningful product signal into a credible surface, while the moment is still alive.

Watched this episode of Dalton + Michael and felt inspired. 
Not by the lawsuit part thankfully, but the idea that startups are basically...
evidence.text:
Watched this episode of Dalton + Michael and felt inspired. 
Not by the lawsuit part thankfully, but the idea that startups are basically risk-transfer entities.

You don’t expect the big Googles to take that level of risk, and they shouldn’t. That’s what startups are for.

For insurance this is even more literally true.
When people ask “why wouldn’t a big carrier build this new insurance line?” the answer is often “why would they put that risk on their balance sheet before it’s been de-risked?”

that’s what startups like @klaimee_ai  are for: absorbing the new AI risk, de-risking the category, and building the market before the big dogs come in.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8pvgN1j-Ck

evidence.originalText:
The weirdest content meeting is the one where everyone remembers a different post winning.

Someone swears the HN post brought the serious buyers.

Someone else remembers the LinkedIn demo getting all the right comments.

Then X enters the chat with one tiny post that somehow sent qualified people to the founder’s profile.

Everyone has screenshots. Nobody has a loop.

For technical teams, that gets expensive fast. You ship, explain the work, post across a few surfaces, then start over from memory the next week.

Memoir’s content performance view is for that moment.

After posts go out across X, LinkedIn, and Hacker News, Memoir helps the team see which content types are actually working. Which topics create real attention. Which formats get technical people to lean in. Which pieces create discussion instead of drive-by likes.

The dashboard is not the interesting part. The learning loop is.

Each published asset becomes evidence for the next one. The product work creates the proof. Memoir carries that proof into the founder’s voice, then helps the team understand what earned attention.

That is how a shipping team stops treating distribution like a weekly reset.

The future I want is simple. Every technical team should know what their market responds to as clearly as they know what they shipped.

evidence.originalText:
There is a company that owns a piece of almost every large public company in America.

Most people have never knowingly bought a single thing from it.

It manages $13.9 trillion. Only the United States and China produce more in a year than it manages for other people.

Here is the strange part. It does not pick hot stocks. It does not promise to beat the market. It mostly sells something very boring and very cheap: funds that simply track the market for a fee as low as 0.03%. That is about thirty cents a year on every $1,000.

So how does a company that earns so little per dollar become one of the most powerful forces in all of finance?

That question is the whole story of BlackRock. And the answer has less to do with investing than you might think, and far more to do with a piece of software called Aladdin.

We broke the whole thing down in a simple read: how it makes money, the bull case, the real risks, and how it stacks up against Vanguard.

Full breakdown linked below.

evidence.originalText:
Eden is building instantly deployable robots-as-a-service for warehouses and factories.

Industrial robotics has historically been difficult to deploy. Customers often need to buy expensive hardware upfront, hire onsite engineers, spend weeks integrating systems, and redesign workflows around robots before seeing value. This has made automation too slow, too expensive, and too rigid for many real-world operations.

Today we're launching Eden-1, an industrial semi-humanoid robot for warehouse and factory work, and Theta a new shared-autonomy robotics foundation model. Eden-1 can be immediately deployed into industrial environments without onsite engineers, long integration cycles, or upfront robot purchases. Customers get robot employees and pay them by the hour.

Our goal is to reimagine services in the upcoming age of autonomy.

In 1.5 months we designed and built our own hardware, model and deployment infrastructure all tightly integrated to achieve one thing...a delightful customer experience.

evidence.originalText:
Learn more: https://gigacatalyst.com/ 
Talk to founder: https://cal.com/namanyayg/yc-priority-call 

Give your sales and CS teams superpowers to build missing features, so you win more deals, increase stickiness, and ship faster

TL;DR: Gigacatalyst allows sales and CS teams to build missing features that customers need, so you stop losing business because of feature gaps. We’ve helped our customers unblock $1M in sales in 6 weeks.

In some B2B software businesses - especially the ones that sit inside a customer’s day-to-day operations - sales and renewals often come down to a few very specific “can it work the way we work?” questions. When the product can’t do that without custom work or a workaround, the buyer assumes the rollout will be painful and the team won’t use it. So prospects end up choosing incumbents which have the needed features, or customers adopt only part of the product and eventually churn.

This creates three compounding problems:

1. You lose competitive deals — customers choose vendors that have the exact workflow they operate on.

2. Customers don’t fully adopt — they buy, but the product doesn’t match how they actually work. So they build workarounds and usage stays low, affecting renewals.

3. Your backlog fills with one-off requests — when you sell to many different types of companies, each customer needs something slightly different.

How Gigacatalyst Works

Gigacatalyst embeds directly inside your SaaS product, built on your APIs and design system and governed by your auth and security. Your customers and team members can build new missing workflows in natural language.

- A Solutions Engineer types "Build a KPI dashboard for maintenance performance" → working dashboard on real data in ~1 minute

- A customer asks for "a photo upload tab that OCRs asset labels and creates a record" → deployed without waiting for engineers

- A vertical enterprise needs "custom lifecycle tracking" → delivered in minutes, not quarters

Each built app runs in a sandbox and inherits your existing auth and RBAC. Everything is native, governed, and shareable.

We deploy an AI builder that learns your platform’s APIs, data model, and design language to every team member so sales, customer success, and product teams can directly ship features without needing to deal with engineers.

We reverse engineer your software's APIs so anyone can build features on par with what already is in your frontend. We put access to that API and data model behind a proxy layer so it is safe and can be constrained and guard-railed exactly how the software company wants it to be. 

Any functionality that is created is built into a sandboxed environment so it does not touch the main codebase or break the main app. We ship each functionality as an “app” and individual apps can be deployed to specific tenants or to multiple tenants within a few clicks.

We allow creating new functionality very easily in a guardrailed environment that can't break the main codebase and can deliver useful workflows. This helps sales, customer success, and product teams. We make building, deployment, and sharing across teams all possible within a web-based interface within a few clicks, making us the easiest platform to build new features by non-engineers. 

Results

- $1M+ in pipeline unblocked in 6 weeks

- 70% day-30 retention

- $100K in churn prevented

- 800+ features shipped in 6 weeks (~2,400 engineering hours equivalent)

Learn more: https://gigacatalyst.com/
Talk to founder: https://cal.com/namanyayg/yc-priority-call

evidence.originalText:
We started giving 500 credits away for new Runtime users.

Someone spent 4 hours trying to hack us. They couldn’t.

Prompt injections in English. Then in Chinese. Curled internal endpoints, echoed env vars, tried to use tokens outside the sandbox. 

Even switched to dark mode halfway through. As if that would help.

Our sandbox proxy encrypts all secrets so they never enter the sandbox. The agent only sees a short-lived token that’s session-scoped, credit-metered, and expires in minutes. Even if you extract it, you get a 402.

Coding agents can be manipulated to do malicious things even when prompted in good faith. 

A user with sandbox access can instruct the agent to exfiltrate credentials or probe internal services.

This is why every session in Runtime is isolated, metered, and logged. The agent never touches real credentials.

If you’re deploying coding agents without this layer, a single prompt injection turns your AI into an attack vector.

evidence.text: Hyperscalers will spend roughly $700 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, more than 60% above last year. Almost none of it reaches the people whose lives become the training data. Today we raised Hub's base contributor rate 25%. Permanently. Every approved hour of real-world data now pays $5.00, up from $4.00. This is a supply decision, not a marketing one. The context matters. This month Kenya published draft rules establishing fair-pay references for AI data workers, following years of documented rates in the low single digits per hour. Regulators are starting to treat data labor as labor.
evidence.originalText:
Hyperscalers will spend roughly $700 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, more than 60% above last year.

Almost none of it reaches the people whose lives become the training data.

Today we raised Hub's base contributor rate 25%. Permanently. Every approved hour of real-world data now pays $5.00, up from $4.00.

This is a supply decision, not a marketing one.

The context matters. This month Kenya published draft rules establishing fair-pay references for AI data workers, following years of documented rates in the low single digits per hour. Regulators are starting to treat data labor as labor. That shift is overdue, and it is going to reshape how this industry sources human input.

Hub sits in a different part of the stack than annotation or moderation. Our contributors do not label someone else's dataset. They create original data that does not exist yet: first-person recordings of real tasks in real homes, the physical-world footage robotics teams cannot obtain any other way.

That work is skilled. Framing, lighting, following a spec precisely, doing it consistently. Networks that underpay lose people exactly when those people get good at it, and quality collapses with them. Retention is upstream of data quality, and pay is upstream of retention.

The next decade of AI will be built on human experience. What that experience is worth is a decision someone makes, not a market accident.

We made ours today.

#RealWorldData #AI #Robotics #AIEthics #DataInfrastructure

evidence.title: The June Secured Finance Network webinar on fraud risk opened with a line worth sitting with.
evidence.text:
The June Secured Finance Network webinar on fraud risk opened with a line worth sitting with.

"As ERPs evolve, payments go fully digital, and bad actors deploy generative AI, traditional monitoring tools are no longer enough."

That's not a warning about the future. It's a description of right now.

Here's what that means in practice for a factoring desk running standard document review:

The fraud that used to take weeks to engineer now takes hours. A borrower who wants to manufacture a receivable can use generative AI to produce an invoice in correct formatting, plausible buyer name, consistent with the borrower's historical style, all in minutes. The document passes visual inspection because it was designed to.

Your analyst reviews it. Approves it. You fund.

The fraud detection gap isn't analyst skill. It's detection architecture. Manual review was built for a world where fraud required significant effort to produce. That world ended.

The checks that now matter can't be run by eye:

Metadata validation: does the file's creation date match the stated invoice date?
Cross-portfolio duplicate detection: was this same receivable submitted to another lender this week?
Buyer registry verification: does this entity actually exist and operate at this scale?
Relationship plausibility: does the transaction size match the buyer-seller history?

None of these take more than seconds when automated. All of them take longer than a typical review cycle when done manually, which means they don't get done.

The cost of a funded fraudulent invoice isn't a write-down. It's a realized loss. And when the LP asks for the audit trail, the question won't be whether fraud occurred. It'll be whether the system was designed to catch it.

Most operations today are running detection designed for the last generation of fraud.

The current generation of fraud was designed with that in mind.
Let’s change this together. Hit us up at hi@zolvo.com

evidence.title: The Iran war caused the largest oil supply disruption in history.
evidence.text:
The Iran war caused the largest oil supply disruption in history. Most people assumed the stock market would crash.

It didn't.

When the Strait of Hormuz, the route for roughly a fifth of the world's oil, was blocked, oil ran from around $73 to nearly $120, then fell all the way back to where it started. A full round trip in months. And through all of it, US markets stayed calm and even touched record highs.

So where did the damage actually go?

Not the stock ticker. Prices. US inflation climbed from 2.4% before the war to over 4%. Fuel, shipping, and food all moved with it.

There's a lesson in that for anyone who follows markets: equities tend to look past a shock they believe is temporary. What they fear is duration, how long higher costs linger and feed inflation. The war made the headlines. The inflation is what quietly stayed.

We broke the whole story down in detail, link in the comments.

For educational purposes only. Not investment advice. Figures approximate.
#iranwar #globalmarkets #marketcrash

evidence.title: Token usage billing has become unsustainable in most teams where adoption is growing while frontier models have had a steady increase in ...
evidence.text:
Token usage billing has become unsustainable in most teams where adoption is growing while frontier models have had a steady increase in price the past years. Even companies like Cursor are managing costs by shifting more usage to their own frontier models while moving away from being the "Costco of tokens".

The best value today comes from using a heavily subsidized plan from a frontier lab like Chatgpt and Claude. But this inherently diminishes freedom of choice as you must either commit to one provider or pay for multiple subscriptions just to use other models.

At enterprise scale, we’ve seen that the lock-in gets even worse as companies are pushed into expensive Chatgpt or Claude Enterprise plans, with workflows, permissioning, and procurement all baked into one stack. However, the problem is that nobody knows what the best frontier model provider will be in a year, a month, or even a week

Token usage billing has become unsustainable in most teams where adoption is growing while frontier models have had a steady increase in price the past years. Even companies like Cursor are managing costs by shifting more usage to their own frontier models while moving away from being the "Costco of tokens".

The best value today comes from using a heavily subsidized plan from a frontier lab like Chatgpt and Claude. But this inherently diminishes freedom of choice as you must either commit to one provider or pay for multiple subscriptions just to use other models.

At enterprise scale, we’ve seen that the lock-in gets even worse as companies are pushed into expensive Chatgpt or Claude Enterprise plans, with workflows, permissioning, and procurement all baked into one stack. However, the problem is that nobody knows what the best frontier model provider will be in a year, a month, or even a week

evidence.title: The June issue of The Secured Lender ran a piece titled "Protecting Collateral Liquidity Through Cyber Operational Resilience." One paragraph has been circulating in ABL circles si
evidence.text:
The June issue of The Secured Lender ran a piece titled "Protecting Collateral Liquidity Through Cyber Operational Resilience." One paragraph has been circulating in ABL circles since.

"In a cyber incident, collateral may remain 'there' but visibility to the lender's collateral and its quality disappears. If a borrower can't ship, can't invoice, or can't produce a trustworthy borrowing base for even a few days, collateral proceeds and AR/inventory mix will change significantly."

That's the hidden operational risk almost no servicing team models for.

Here's the structure of the problem:

ABL is built on the premise that collateral converts to cash if the borrower defaults. But that conversion depends on a live, accurate picture of what the collateral actually is at any given moment. AR aging. Invoice mix. Inventory levels. Dilution rates.

When that picture goes dark, whether because of a cyber incident, a system failure, or simply a manual process that can't update fast enough, the lender is flying without instruments.

The borrowing base certificate becomes stale the moment it's submitted. By the time the next one arrives, the collateral composition has already shifted. A lender relying on periodic manual reporting is always operating on a lag.

The operational consequence isn't theoretical. It shows up in advance rate calculations that don't reflect current eligibility. In concentration limits that breach silently. In covenant monitoring that catches problems after they've compounded.

The lenders who aren't exposed to this risk aren't running better field exams. They're running continuous monitoring: real-time data feeds from bank accounts and receivables systems, automatic borrowing base recalculation, covenant alerts that fire before breach rather than after.

The infrastructure gap between a periodic manual process and a continuous one is where most collateral risk lives in 2026. Not in credit quality, in visibility latency.

evidence.title: General Instinct - The deployment layer for physical intelligence
evidence.text: TL;DR: General Instinct deploy frontier AI models onto constrained edge hardware for robots, drones, and physical AI systems. Problem: Physical AI (robots, drones, IoT) teams can now get frontier models to do impressive things in the lab. The hard part is getting those models to work reliably in production. Some common patterns: 1. Models works well in the cloud, but fails on edge in production. 2. Custom use-cases like robots operating in the wild or in space requires on device inference. 3. Using Gemini for everything is simply too expensive. We built a custom, no code pipeline to solve this
evidence.originalText:
TL;DR: 
General Instinct deploy frontier AI models onto constrained edge hardware for robots, drones, and physical AI systems.

Problem:

Physical AI (robots, drones, IoT) teams can now get frontier models to do impressive things in the lab. The hard part is getting those models to work reliably in production.

Some common patterns:

1. Models works well in the cloud, but fails on edge in production.

2. Custom use-cases like robots operating in the wild or in space requires on device inference.

3. Using Gemini for everything is simply too expensive.

We built a custom, no code pipeline to solve this problem.

What we’re building:

Our first product: Instinct Edge. Give us a model, a target device, and a latency budget. We return an offline runtime that hits the budget on hardware like Jetson, mobile NPUs, ARM CPUs, Apple Neural Engine, and Snapdragons.

Under the hood, this combines compression recipes, custom CUDA / Metal / ARM NEON kernels, and a continuous data-to-serving pipeline.

One production example: a multimodal classifier on Jetson Orin NX with 111 ms cold start, 100% of decisions inside a 150 ms budget, and zero cloud calls.

How you can help:

If you or anyone you know are running large vision models on edge and are having problems fitting them onto your hardware, let us know by emailing founders@general-instinct.com!

evidence.title: Skip git worktrees.
evidence.text: Skip git worktrees. Go straight to micro-VMs. Everyone's discovering worktrees for running parallel agents. But also figuring out why they are so annoying to work with. Worktrees solve branch isolation but inherit every limitation of your local machine. Port conflicts, dependency clashes, secrets leaking between sessions. Four agents in parallel and your laptop is cooked. I spin up an ephemeral micro-VM per agent session. Dependencies pre-installed, secrets injected, own ports, own preview URL. The only set up required is snapshotting your environment once. It then rebuilds on every change to main. Every new agent session boots from that snapshot in milliseconds. This is how I'm running 20+ parallel agent sessions this way. Even Cursor and Conductor are now moving agent workflows to the cloud.
